title: Professional Responsibility Practice Finals
description: One practice final of 90 questions, sized like the real final (closed book, 90 multiple-choice questions in 180 minutes) and covering Weeks 1–15 in outline order: regulating lawyers, the client-lawyer relationship, confidentiality, fiduciary duty and authority, fees and client funds, conflicts, government lawyers and prosecutors, advocacy, firms and organizational clients, public service, duties to third parties, advertising, and MR 8.4(g). New MPRE-style fact patterns with five choices; every choice is explained, and every Model Rule cite opens the rule text.

exams.title: Final 1
exams.description: 90 questions in outline order, Weeks 1–15 (Burk Chs. 1–25 and the Model Rules).

questions.area: Sources of Law and the Model Rules
questions.q: Client Carla sues Lawyer Leo for malpractice after a business deal Leo arranged between them goes bad. Leo never advised Carla in writing to get independent counsel, as Rule 1.8(a)(2) requires. Carla's complaint alleges that the violation of Rule 1.8(a) establishes Leo's negligence as a matter of law. How is the court most likely to treat the rule violation?
o: It establishes Leo's breach of duty as a matter of law, because the Model Rules define the duty of care a lawyer owes a client.
It does not by itself create liability, but the court may consider the rule as evidence of the standard of care.
It is irrelevant to the civil claim, because the Model Rules may be used only by disciplinary authorities.
It creates a rebuttable presumption that Leo breached a duty, shifting the burden of proof to him.
It supports the claim only if the state bar has first disciplined Leo for the same conduct.
oe: That is a negligence-per-se theory. The Scope rejects it: a Rule violation does not itself give rise to a cause of action, and the duty of care comes from tort and agency law.

Correct. The Scope says a violation "should not itself give rise to a cause of action" or create a presumption that a legal duty was breached, but because the Rules set standards of conduct, a violation may be evidence of breach of the applicable standard. Burk notes most courts admit the Rules for that purpose.
Too strong. The Scope says the Rules are not designed to be a basis for civil liability, but courts may treat a violation as evidence of the standard of conduct.
The Scope expressly says a violation should not "create any presumption" that a legal duty has been breached.
A civil claim does not depend on a disciplinary finding; the two proceedings are independent, and either may go forward without the other.
questions.e: Under the Scope of the Model Rules, violating a Rule (here Rule 1.8(a)) is not itself a cause of action and raises no presumption of breach, but it may be evidence of the standard of care in a civil case.

questions.tag: MR 8.1(a): a lawyer's statements about another applicant
questions.q: Lawyer Lou is asked by the state board of bar examiners to complete a character questionnaire about his longtime friend Fran, who has applied for admission. Lou knows, from their friendship, that Fran was convicted of shoplifting two years ago; Fran left the conviction off her application. The questionnaire asks whether Lou knows of any conduct reflecting on Fran's honesty. Lou answers "No." Is Lou subject to discipline?
o: No, because Rule 8.1 governs only the statements an applicant makes about her own admission.
No, because Lou learned of the conviction in confidence, so Rule 1.6 required him to keep silent.
Yes, but only if the board admits Fran in reliance on his answer.
No, because a shoplifting conviction is a minor offense that is not material to fitness to practice.
Yes, because he knowingly made a false material statement in connection with a bar application.
oe: Rule 8.1 applies to "an applicant for admission to the bar, or a lawyer in connection with a bar admission application." A lawyer vouching for someone else is covered.
Lou is Fran's friend, not her lawyer, so Rule 1.6 does not protect what he knows. And even 1.6-protected information would allow him to decline to answer, never to lie.
Rule 8.1(a) does not require reliance or harm. The knowing false statement of a material fact is the violation.
Shoplifting is a crime of dishonesty, which bears directly on character and fitness. A question asking about honesty makes it material.

Correct. Rule 8.1(a) bars a lawyer, "in connection with a bar admission application," from knowingly making a false statement of material fact. Rule 8.1, Comment [1] confirms the duty covers statements about other applicants, not just the lawyer's own.
questions.e: Rule 8.1(a) forbids knowing false statements of material fact by applicants and by lawyers "in connection with a bar admission application," including character references for others; Rule 8.1(b) adds a duty to correct known misapprehensions.

questions.tag: MR 8.4(b): violent misdemeanor unrelated to practice
questions.q: At a neighborhood cookout, Lawyer Dana gets into a shouting match with a neighbor over a property line and punches him, breaking his nose. Dana pleads guilty to misdemeanor battery and pays a fine. The incident had nothing to do with her law practice. Is Dana subject to discipline?
o: No, because only felonies can be the basis of professional discipline under Rule 8.4(b).
No, because the battery occurred in her private life and had no connection to any client or matter.
Yes, because any criminal conviction of a lawyer is professional misconduct under Rule 8.4(b).
No, because Rule 8.4(b) reaches only crimes involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation.
Yes, because a crime of violence reflects adversely on a lawyer's fitness.
oe: Rule 8.4(b) turns on whether the criminal act reflects adversely on fitness, not on whether it is a felony or a misdemeanor.
Rule 8.4(b) covers private conduct. Comment [2] explains that a lawyer is answerable for offenses showing a lack of characteristics relevant to practice, and violence is one.

Right result, wrong reason. Comment [2] says a lawyer should be professionally answerable only for offenses that indicate lack of the characteristics relevant to law practice, such as violence or dishonesty, not for every crime.
Dishonesty is the separate ground in Rule 8.4(c). Rule 8.4(b) also covers crimes that reflect on "fitness as a lawyer in other respects," which include crimes of violence.

Correct. Rule 8.4(b) reaches a criminal act that reflects adversely on honesty, trustworthiness "or fitness as a lawyer in other respects." Rule 8.4, Comment [2] lists offenses involving violence among those that qualify, whether or not they occur in practice.
questions.e: Rule 8.4(b) makes it misconduct to commit a criminal act reflecting adversely on honesty, trustworthiness or fitness; Rule 8.4, Comment [2] puts violence, dishonesty, breach of trust and serious interference with justice in that category, along with a pattern of minor offenses.

questions.tag: MR 5.5(c)(4): temporary work arising from home practice
questions.q: Lawyer Priya is admitted only in Pennsylvania. Her longtime Pennsylvania client is buying a warehouse in Delaware, and Priya spends four days in Wilmington negotiating the purchase agreement with the seller's Delaware counsel. She does not associate with a Delaware lawyer, does not hold herself out as admitted in Delaware, and returns home when the deal closes. Is Priya engaged in the unauthorized practice of law?
o: Yes, because a lawyer may not practice law in a jurisdiction where she is not admitted.
Yes, unless she associates with a Delaware lawyer who actively participates in the matter.
No, because the work is temporary and arises out of her practice in a jurisdiction where she is admitted.
No, because a lawyer admitted in any state may practice anywhere in the country so long as she is competent.
Yes, because negotiating the agreement in person in Delaware establishes a continuous presence there.
oe: That is the general rule of Rule 5.5(a), but Rule 5.5(c) carves out temporary practice in four situations, and Priya fits Rule 5.5(c)(4).
Association with local counsel is one safe harbor, Rule 5.5(c)(1), but the four safe harbors are alternatives; any one suffices.

Correct. Rule 5.5(c)(4) lets a lawyer admitted elsewhere provide legal services on a temporary basis that arise out of or are reasonably related to the lawyer's practice in a jurisdiction where she is admitted. A Pennsylvania client's deal fits.
There is no national license. Rule 5.5(b) forbids a systematic and continuous presence or holding out in a state where the lawyer isn't admitted; only temporary work under Rule 5.5(c) is allowed.
A four-day trip for one transaction is temporary. A systematic and continuous presence under Rule 5.5(b) means something like an office or an ongoing practice in the state.
questions.e: Rule 5.5(c) allows temporary practice by a lawyer admitted elsewhere when any one of four conditions holds: (1) association with active local counsel, (2) a pending or expected proceeding where she is or expects to be authorized to appear, (3) a related ADR proceeding, or (4) work arising out of or reasonably related to her home practice.

questions.tag: MR 8.5: disciplinary authority and choice of law
questions.q: Lawyer Nate is admitted only in New York. He is admitted pro hac vice to defend a client in a trial in a New Jersey state court. During the trial he engages in conduct that violates New Jersey's Rules of Professional Conduct but would not violate New York's. Which statement is most accurate?
o: Only New Jersey may discipline Nate, because the conduct occurred in a New Jersey proceeding.
New York may discipline Nate, but it must apply New York's rules because he is admitted only there.
Both states may discipline Nate, and each should apply New Jersey's rules.
Neither state may discipline Nate; a pro hac vice lawyer answers only to the trial court's contempt power.
New Jersey may discipline Nate, applying New York's rules, because those are the rules he was licensed under.
oe: Rule 8.5(a) gives New York authority over its own admittees "regardless of where the lawyer's conduct occurs," so both states may act.
Rule 8.5(b)(1) sends conduct before a tribunal to the rules where the tribunal sits, so even New York applies New Jersey's rules.

Correct. Under Rule 8.5(a) Nate is subject to discipline where he is admitted (New York) and where he provides legal services (New Jersey). Under Rule 8.5(b)(1), conduct in a matter pending before a tribunal is judged by the rules of the jurisdiction where the tribunal sits, here New Jersey.
Rule 8.5(a) subjects a lawyer to discipline in any jurisdiction where he provides or offers legal services, which includes a pro hac vice appearance.
Under Rule 8.5(b)(1) the governing rules for conduct before a tribunal are those of the tribunal's jurisdiction, not the lawyer's home state.
questions.e: Rule 8.5(a) lets both the licensing state and any state where the lawyer provides services discipline him; Rule 8.5(b)(1) applies the rules of the tribunal's jurisdiction to conduct in a pending matter, and Rule 8.5(b)(2) uses the place of conduct or its predominant effect otherwise.

questions.area: Consequences: Civil Liability, Sanctions, and Other Law
questions.q: Lawyer Ross once represented Alpha Corp. in negotiating its distribution contracts. Now Ross sues Alpha for Beta Corp., claiming that those same contracts violate the antitrust laws. Alpha moves to disqualify Ross. Ross argues that the motion must be denied because Alpha cannot show that he has actually used any of its confidential information, and because no disciplinary authority has found that he violated the Rules. How should the court rule?
o: Deny the motion, because only the state's disciplinary authority may enforce the Rules of Professional Conduct.
Deny the motion unless Alpha proves that Ross has actually revealed or used its confidential information.
Grant the motion, but only after a disciplinary proceeding determines that Ross violated Rule 1.9.
Deny the motion, because disqualification is available only for conflicts between two current clients.
Grant the motion, because disqualification protects the former client's confidences without proof that they were used.
oe: Courts regulate the lawyers appearing before them and routinely use the Rules as the standard for disqualification motions, independent of discipline.
Requiring proof of actual misuse would force the former client to reveal the very confidences it seeks to protect. The substantial-relationship test presumes access instead.
Disqualification is a civil remedy the court decides for itself; it doesn't wait on a disciplinary finding.
Former-client conflicts under Rule 1.9 are among the most common grounds for disqualification.

Correct. Courts disqualify under their inherent power to supervise the lawyers before them. Disqualification is prophylactic: when the matters are the same or substantially related under Rule 1.9(a), the court presumes the lawyer has confidential information that could be used, without requiring proof of actual misuse or any prior disciplinary finding.
questions.e: Disqualification is a court-imposed, prophylactic remedy: it rests on the court's inherent power, uses the Rules (here Rule 1.9(a)) as its standard, and does not require proof that confidences were actually misused or a prior disciplinary finding.

questions.area: Consequences: Civil Liability, Sanctions, and Other Law
questions.tag: Inherent-power fee sanctions must be compensatory
questions.q: After a two-year product-liability case, a federal judge finds that defense counsel withheld key test results in bad faith during discovery. Using its inherent power, the court orders the defendant and its lawyers to pay every dollar of attorney's fees the plaintiffs incurred from the day the suit was filed. On appeal, what is the most likely result?
o: The award will be affirmed, because bad-faith discovery misconduct permits the court to shift all fees in the case.
The award will be reversed, because only a disciplinary authority may sanction lawyers for discovery misconduct.
The award will be reversed, because a court's inherent power permits sanctions only against parties, not their lawyers.
The award will be limited to the fees the plaintiffs would not have incurred but for the misconduct.
The award will be affirmed in full, because a punitive fee award deters other lawyers from similar conduct.
oe: Goodyear Tire & Rubber rejected an award untethered to causation; a court may shift all fees only if all of them were caused by the misconduct.
Courts have their own sanctioning powers, including FRCP 37, FRCP 11, 28 U.S.C. § 1927 and their inherent power, alongside discipline under Rule 3.4(d).
Inherent-power sanctions can run against lawyers as well as parties; the limit Goodyear imposes is on amount, not on who pays.

Correct. In Goodyear Tire & Rubber Co. v. Haeger (2017), the Supreme Court held that a fee award under a court's inherent power must be compensatory, not punitive, and so is limited to fees caused by the misconduct under a but-for standard.
Goodyear Tire & Rubber holds that a punitive award would require criminal-type procedural protections; in civil sanctions, the fee award must compensate for harm the misconduct caused.
questions.e: Court sanctions are a separate track from discipline; fee sanctions under inherent power must be compensatory and limited to fees the misconduct caused (Goodyear Tire & Rubber), and discovery abuse can also violate Rule 3.4(d).

questions.area: Why Smart People Do Stupid Things (Ch. 4)
questions.q: First-year associate Amir is preparing a document production. Partner Paula tells him to leave out an email that is plainly responsive to the other side's requests, explaining, "It's how this firm wins cases, and I'll take the heat." Amir is uneasy but complies, reasoning that Paula is the senior lawyer on the matter. Is Amir subject to discipline?
o: No, because a subordinate lawyer who acts at a supervisor's direction is protected by Rule 5.2(b).
Yes, because a lawyer must follow the Rules even when acting at another lawyer's direction.
No, because only Paula, as the partner who ordered the omission, is responsible under Rule 5.1(c).
Yes, but only if Amir knew that the email would harm Paula's client's position in the case.
No, because new lawyers are held to a lower standard while they learn the norms of their firm.
oe: Rule 5.2(b) protects only reliance on a supervisor's reasonable resolution of an arguable question of professional duty. Hiding a plainly responsive email is neither reasonable nor arguable.

Correct. Rule 5.2(a) makes a subordinate bound by the Rules "notwithstanding that the lawyer acted at the direction of another person." The Rule 5.2(b) safe harbor covers only a supervisor's reasonable resolution of an arguable question, and suppressing a plainly responsive document is not arguable (Rule 3.4(a), (d)).
Rule 5.1(c) can make Paula responsible too, but it doesn't relieve Amir. Both can be disciplined.
The violation is obstructing access to evidence and failing to comply with a proper discovery request under Rule 3.4(a) and (d); harm to the client is beside the point.
The Rules have no lower standard for new lawyers. Burk's point about situational pressure is that it explains such lapses, not that it excuses them.
questions.e: Under Rule 5.2(a) a subordinate who violates the Rules at a supervisor's direction is still responsible; Rule 5.2(b) protects only reliance on a supervisor's reasonable resolution of an arguable question.

questions.tag: MR 1.0(b), (n): confirmed in writing by email
questions.q: Lawyer Grace explains a conflict of interest to her client by phone, and the client gives informed consent. The next morning Grace sends the client an email summarizing the conflict and stating that the client consented. The client never replies. Has the consent been "confirmed in writing" under the Model Rules?
o: Yes, because the lawyer may confirm an oral consent by promptly transmitting a writing, and an email is a writing.
No, because a consent is confirmed in writing only when the client signs the confirming document.
No, because the client must reply to the email to show that the client agrees with the summary.
No, because an email is not a "writing" unless it carries an electronic signature.
Yes, but only because the client's failure to object is itself informed consent to the conflict.
oe: Correct. Rule 1.0(b) defines "confirmed in writing" to include "a writing that a lawyer promptly transmits to the person confirming an oral informed consent," and Rule 1.0(n) says a writing includes an electronic communication such as email.
A client signature is required only where a rule says "in a writing signed by the client," as in Rule 1.8(a) and (g) or Rule 1.5(c). Rule 1.0(b) does not require one.
Rule 1.0(b) is satisfied by the lawyer's prompt transmission of the confirming writing; no reply is required.
Rule 1.0(n) defines a writing as a tangible or electronic record, including email; a signature is relevant only when a rule calls for a signed writing.
The client's informed consent came on the phone call. Silence is not consent; the email only confirms what the client already agreed to.
questions.e: "Confirmed in writing" (Rule 1.0(b)) means informed consent given in writing by the person, or an oral consent that the lawyer promptly confirms in a writing sent to the person; email counts as a writing (Rule 1.0(n)).

questions.q: Lawyer Lena practices residential real estate. A longtime client asks her to register a trademark for the client's new bakery, something Lena has never done. Lena tells the client she has not handled trademarks before, spends several evenings studying the process, and arranges with the client's consent to have an experienced trademark lawyer review her filing. Was it proper for Lena to accept the matter?
o: No, because a lawyer who lacks experience in a field must decline the matter or refer it to a specialist.
Yes, because a lawyer can become competent in a new field through study or by associating an expert.
Yes, but only if she bills the client nothing for the hours she spent learning trademark law.
No, because a trademark registration requires specialized knowledge that only a certified specialist may provide.
Yes, because Rule 1.1 applies only to litigation, where a lack of skill can prejudice the client in court.
oe: Rule 1.1, Comment [2] rejects that view: a lawyer need not have special training or prior experience to handle a problem of a type with which she is unfamiliar.

Correct. Rule 1.1, Comment [2] says a lawyer can provide adequate representation in a wholly novel field through necessary study, and Comment [4] adds that competence can be achieved by reasonable preparation. Associating a lawyer of established competence is another route.
How she bills is a Rule 1.5(a) reasonableness question; it is not a condition of competence under Rule 1.1.
Nothing in Rule 1.1 limits trademark work to specialists. Competence is the knowledge, skill, thoroughness and preparation reasonably necessary, however acquired.
Rule 1.1 applies to all representation, transactional as well as litigation.
questions.e: Rule 1.1 requires the legal knowledge, skill, thoroughness and preparation reasonably necessary; Comments [2] and [4] allow a lawyer to reach competence in an unfamiliar area through study, preparation, or association with an experienced lawyer.

questions.area: The Civil Duty of Care and Effective Assistance
questions.tag: Strickland: no prejudice, no ineffective assistance
questions.q: Defense lawyer Dev never interviews an alibi witness his client named, and the client is convicted of robbery. In a later habeas proceeding, the court finds that no reasonable lawyer would have failed to interview the witness, but that the prosecution's evidence (a confession, video footage, and the stolen property found in the client's car) was so strong that the alibi testimony would not have changed the verdict. Has the client shown ineffective assistance of counsel?
o: Yes, because counsel's performance fell below an objective standard of reasonableness.
Yes, because prejudice is presumed whenever defense counsel fails to investigate a named witness.
No, because he cannot show a reasonable probability that the result would have been different.
No, because the Sixth Amendment guarantees only that a licensed lawyer appear for the defendant.
Yes, because a conviction obtained after counsel violated the duty of competence in Rule 1.1 must be vacated.
oe: Deficient performance is only the first Strickland prong. Without prejudice, the claim fails.

United States v. Cronic presumes prejudice only in narrow cases, such as a complete denial of counsel or a total failure to test the prosecution's case. A single investigative failure falls under Strickland.

Correct. Strickland requires both (1) performance below an objective standard of reasonableness and (2) prejudice: a reasonable probability that, but for counsel's errors, the result would have been different. The court found the first but not the second.
The right is to effective assistance; Strickland judges the quality of counsel's performance, not just the presence of a lawyer.
A Rule 1.1 violation may support discipline, but the constitutional standard for vacating a conviction is Strickland's two-part test.
questions.e: Ineffective assistance under Strickland requires (all required) (1) deficient performance measured by prevailing professional norms and (2) prejudice, a reasonable probability of a different result; prejudice is presumed only in the narrow situations of United States v. Cronic.

questions.area: Forming the Relationship and Identifying the Client
questions.q: Wanda meets Lawyer Lyle for an hour at a free consultation and describes how her husband was injured during surgery. Lyle says he doesn't think she has a case and that he won't take it, but he does not mention that a two-year statute of limitations will soon run, or suggest that she consult another lawyer. Relying on his opinion, Wanda does nothing until the limitations period has expired. In a malpractice suit by Wanda, what is the most likely result?
o: Lyle is not liable, because he declined the representation, so no lawyer-client relationship ever existed.
Lyle is not liable, because Wanda paid nothing for the consultation.
Lyle may be liable, because by giving advice he formed a relationship that required reasonable care.
Lyle is liable only if Wanda shows he intended to mislead her about the merits of her claim.
Lyle is not liable, because a lawyer owes no duties at all to a person who consults him only as a prospective client.
oe: Declining the matter did not prevent the relationship Togstad recognized: the lawyer gave legal advice on which the person reasonably relied.
A lawyer-client relationship does not require a fee; it can arise from advice given and reasonably relied upon.

Correct. In Togstad, the court found a lawyer-client relationship where the lawyer gave legal advice in an initial consultation and the person reasonably relied on it. Advice given carelessly, without warning about the limitations period, supported liability.
Malpractice is negligence; intent to mislead is not required. Careless advice suffices.
Even a prospective client is owed duties under Rule 1.18, and Togstad shows that advice can turn a consultation into a relationship carrying a duty of care.
questions.e: A lawyer-client relationship can arise by implication when a person seeks advice, the lawyer gives it, and the person reasonably relies (Togstad); when declining, make clear you aren't taking the matter and flag deadlines such as limitations periods.

questions.area: Forming the Relationship and Identifying the Client
questions.q: Without any prior contact, Dmitri finds Lawyer Lucia's firm website, which lists her email address but makes no invitation to submit case details. He sends Lucia a long email describing his plan to sue his business partner and attaching their partnership agreement. Lucia already represents the partner. Is Dmitri a prospective client to whom Lucia owes duties under Rule 1.18?
o: Yes, because anyone who sends a lawyer information about a possible case becomes a prospective client.
Yes, because Lucia's website listed her email address, which invited the public to contact her about matters.
No, because he contacted her unilaterally, without a reasonable expectation of a consultation.
No, because a prospective client must meet the lawyer in person or by phone before Rule 1.18 applies.
Yes, but only if Dmitri marked his email as confidential before sending it.
oe: Rule 1.18, Comment [2] is to the contrary: unilateral communications without a reasonable expectation of a consultation don't create prospective-client status.
Comment [2] treats a website that specifically invites people to submit information about their matters differently from a simple listing of contact information. The latter is not an invitation.

Correct. Rule 1.18, Comment [2] says a person who communicates information unilaterally to a lawyer, without any reasonable expectation that the lawyer is willing to discuss the possibility of forming a relationship, is not a prospective client. A bare listing of an email address does not invite the disclosure.
Rule 1.18 can apply to written or electronic communications; the question is whether there was a consultation, not the medium.
A confidentiality label does not by itself create a reasonable expectation that the lawyer was willing to consult.
questions.e: A prospective client under Rule 1.18(a) is someone who consults with a lawyer about forming a relationship; Comment [2] excludes a person who communicates unilaterally without a reasonable expectation that the lawyer is willing to discuss it.

questions.area: Scope of the Engagement and Duties to Non-Clients
questions.tag: MR 1.2(c): reasonable limited scope with informed consent
questions.q: Lawyer Ben agrees to review a lease for a small-business client for a flat fee of $300, on the condition that he will look only at the rent and renewal clauses and not at the rest of the 40-page document. He explains what he will and won't review and the risks of leaving the other provisions unexamined, and the client agrees. Is the limitation proper?
o: No, because a lawyer who reviews a document must review all of it to meet the duty of competence.
Yes, but only if the client confirms the limitation in a writing signed by the client.
No, because a lawyer may not limit the scope of a representation to reduce the fee.
Yes, without any further step, because the client is a business and is presumed to understand the risks.
Yes, if the limitation is reasonable under the circumstances and the client gives informed consent.
oe: Competence under Rule 1.1 is measured against the agreed scope; Rule 1.2(c) lets the client and lawyer limit that scope, so long as the limitation is reasonable.
Rule 1.2(c) requires informed consent, not a signed writing. A writing is wise but not required by the Rule.
Limited-scope arrangements are often used precisely to make services affordable; Rule 1.2, Comment [7] permits them when reasonable.
Rule 1.2(c) requires informed consent from every client, which means the lawyer must explain the material risks and alternatives under Rule 1.0(e).

Correct. Rule 1.2(c) permits limiting the scope of a representation "if the limitation is reasonable under the circumstances and the client gives informed consent." Ben explained the limits and risks, which is what informed consent under Rule 1.0(e) requires.
questions.e: Rule 1.2(c): a lawyer may limit the scope of a representation if (all required) (1) the limitation is reasonable under the circumstances and (2) the client gives informed consent; Nichols shows the malpractice risk of failing to explain what's left out.

questions.area: Scope of the Engagement and Duties to Non-Clients
questions.q: Lawyer Wes drafts a will for Testator Tom that is meant to leave Tom's lake house to his niece Nina. Because Wes uses a form of devise that the state's law invalidates, the gift fails and the house passes to Tom's estranged son. Nina was never Wes's client. If Nina sues Wes for malpractice, what is the most likely result?
o: Nina may recover, because a lawyer drafting a will owes a duty of care to the intended beneficiary.
Nina cannot recover, because a lawyer owes a duty of care only to persons in privity with the lawyer.
Nina cannot recover, because only Tom's estate, as the client's successor, may sue Wes.
Nina may recover only if she shows Wes deliberately defeated the gift.
Nina may recover, because a lawyer owes all non-clients the same duty of care owed to clients.
oe: Correct. Lucas v. Hamm held that a lawyer who drafts a will can be liable to an intended beneficiary harmed by the lawyer's negligence, though the beneficiary was not the client; the testator's purpose was to benefit her.
Strict privity is the old rule that Lucas and many courts relaxed for intended beneficiaries of the lawyer's work.
The estate may have a claim, but courts following Lucas allow the intended beneficiary to sue as well, since she is the one harmed.
Liability to an intended beneficiary rests on negligence; intent is not required.
Too broad. Lawyers owe non-clients a duty of care only in limited situations, such as when the client's purpose is to benefit the non-client or the non-client is invited to rely.
questions.e: Lawyers can owe a duty of care to non-clients in limited settings, most commonly the intended beneficiaries of a will (Lucas) and third parties invited to rely on the lawyer's work.

questions.tag: MR 1.14(b)–(c): protective action and limited disclosure
questions.q: Lawyer Rosa represents elderly Client Hal in updating his will. During their meetings Rosa reasonably concludes that Hal now has substantial difficulty understanding and evaluating information, and that a new "friend" is pressuring him to sign over his house. Hal cannot be persuaded to deal with the risk himself. Which action may Rosa take under the Model Rules?
o: Consult Hal's adult daughter about protecting him, revealing only what she reasonably believes necessary, and tell Hal she has done so.
Nothing, because revealing any information about Hal without his express consent would violate Rule 1.6.
Withdraw immediately, because a lawyer may not continue to represent a client with decision-making limitations.
Petition at once for a guardian for Hal, because protective action must begin with the most protective measure the court can order.
Report the friend to the police and give them Hal's entire estate plan, because his safety overrides confidentiality.
oe: Correct. Rule 1.14(b) permits reasonably necessary protective action when the lawyer reasonably believes the client (1) has decision-making limitations, (2) is at risk of substantial harm, and (3) cannot adequately act in his own interest. Rule 1.14, Comment [12] lists consulting family members, Rule 1.14(c) limits disclosure to what the lawyer reasonably believes necessary, and Comment [17] requires informing the client of the protective action.
Rule 1.14(c) makes an exception: when taking protective action under Rule 1.14(b), the lawyer may reveal information to the extent she reasonably believes necessary to protect the client's interests.
Rule 1.14(a) requires the lawyer to maintain an ordinary client-lawyer relationship as far as reasonably possible, and Comment [17] says protective action does not by itself require withdrawal.

Guardianship is available in appropriate cases (Rule 1.14, Comment [15]), but Comment [12] tells the lawyer to minimize intrusion into the client's autonomy, so a lesser step such as consulting family usually comes first.
Rule 1.14(c) authorizes only the disclosure the lawyer reasonably believes necessary to protect the client; handing over the whole estate plan goes beyond that.
questions.e: Under Rule 1.14(b), when the lawyer reasonably believes the client (1) has decision-making limitations, (2) is at risk of substantial harm unless action is taken, and (3) cannot adequately act in his own interest (all required), the lawyer may take reasonably necessary protective action; Rule 1.14(c) permits only the disclosure reasonably believed necessary.

questions.q: Client Cal fires Lawyer Lee by email two weeks before a scheduled hearing in a civil case, saying only that he has "lost confidence" in her. Lee believes the firing is unjustified and that she could win the hearing. The court's rules require leave to withdraw from a pending case. What must Lee do?
o: Stop working on the matter at once, because a discharged lawyer has no further duties to the client.
Seek the court's leave to withdraw, and continue the representation if the court orders her to.
Continue the representation through the hearing, because the client has no good cause to discharge her.
Ask the court for leave to withdraw only if Cal confirms the discharge in a signed writing.
Refuse to withdraw until Cal pays her full contingent fee, since he fired her without cause.
oe: Rule 1.16(c) requires the court's permission where its rules demand it, and Rule 1.16(d) imposes exit duties such as protecting the client's interests and returning papers and property.

Correct. Discharge requires withdrawal under Rule 1.16(a)(3), and a client may fire a lawyer at any time, with or without cause (Comment [4]). But under Rule 1.16(c) she must comply with the rule requiring the tribunal's permission, and continue if ordered.
A client may discharge a lawyer at any time, with or without cause; good cause matters only to what fee the lawyer may recover.
Nothing in Rule 1.16 requires a written or signed discharge. An email firing is effective.
Lee may have a claim in quantum meruit, but she may not hold the representation hostage. Rule 1.16(d) requires her to protect Cal's interests on termination.
questions.e: A client may discharge a lawyer at any time (Rule 1.16(a)(3), Comment [4]); the lawyer must still obtain any required leave of the tribunal and continue if ordered (Rule 1.16(c)), then perform the exit duties of Rule 1.16(d).

questions.q: Client Kim has not paid Lawyer Lars's last four monthly invoices in a contract dispute. Lars warned Kim in writing two months ago that he would withdraw unless she paid or made arrangements to pay. She has done neither. No trial date has been set, and withdrawing now would not seriously harm Kim. May Lars withdraw?
o: No, because a lawyer may never withdraw from a pending lawsuit for the client's failure to pay fees.
Yes, but only if he first obtains Kim's informed consent to the withdrawal.
No, because he must keep representing her until he obtains a judgment against her for the unpaid fees.
Yes, and he must withdraw, because continuing to work without payment would be an unreasonable financial burden.
Yes, because Kim has failed substantially to fulfill her obligation to pay after a reasonable warning.
oe: Nonpayment after warning is an express ground for permissive withdrawal in Rule 1.16(b)(5).
Permissive withdrawal under Rule 1.16(b) does not require the client's consent; it requires one of the listed grounds and compliance with Rule 1.16(c) and (d).
Nothing requires a fee judgment before withdrawal; Rule 1.16(b)(5) requires only substantial nonpayment and a reasonable warning.
Withdrawal for nonpayment is permissive, not mandatory. Rule 1.16(a) lists the mandatory grounds, and unpaid fees are not among them.

Correct. Rule 1.16(b)(5) permits withdrawal when the client fails substantially to fulfill an obligation to the lawyer regarding the lawyer's services and has been given reasonable warning that the lawyer will withdraw unless it is fulfilled. Lars must still get any leave the court requires (Rule 1.16(c)).
questions.e: Rule 1.16(b) lists permissive grounds; Rule 1.16(b)(5) allows withdrawal when the client substantially fails to meet an obligation to the lawyer after reasonable warning; tribunal permission under Rule 1.16(c) and exit duties under Rule 1.16(d) still apply.

questions.tag: MR 1.16(d): the file and unearned fees on exit
questions.q: Client Paz discharges Lawyer Lin in the middle of a contract dispute and hires new counsel. Paz had paid Lin a $10,000 advance, of which Lin has earned $6,000. Paz still owes Lin nothing else, but Lin is annoyed at being fired. New counsel asks for Paz's file. Which of the following must Lin do?
o: Keep the entire $10,000, because the client fired her without cause in the middle of the matter.
Return the unearned $4,000 but keep the file until Paz signs a release of any claims against Lin.
Surrender the file but keep the $4,000 as security for any future fees Paz may owe her.
Send the file to new counsel only if the court orders her to do so.
Return the $4,000 unearned balance and surrender the papers and property Paz is entitled to.
oe: Rule 1.16(d) requires refund of the unearned portion of an advance fee; being discharged without cause doesn't change that.
Holding the file hostage for a release prejudices the client and is not a lien permitted by other law; it violates Rule 1.16(d) and invites a Rule 1.8(h)(2) problem.
Paz owes Lin nothing more. Unearned fees belong to the client and must be refunded under Rule 1.16(d) and Rule 1.15(d).
No court order is needed. Rule 1.16(d) itself requires surrendering papers and property to which the client is entitled.

Correct. Rule 1.16(d) requires a lawyer on termination to take reasonable steps to protect the client's interests, including surrendering papers and property to which the client is entitled and refunding any advance payment of a fee or expense that has not been earned or incurred.
questions.e: On termination, Rule 1.16(d) requires reasonable steps to protect the client: notice, time to find other counsel, surrender of papers and property the client is entitled to, and refund of unearned advance fees and unincurred expenses (a lawyer may keep papers only as other law permits).

questions.q: Lawyer Tess represented Client Omar in a lawsuit that was widely reported in the local paper, including Omar's admission at trial that he had filed for bankruptcy years earlier. After the case ends, Tess mentions Omar's bankruptcy to a friend at dinner, pointing out that "it was all in the newspaper anyway." Omar has not consented. Is Tess subject to discipline?
o: No, because the information was disclosed in open court and so is no longer confidential.
No, because the duty of confidentiality ends when the representation ends.
Yes, but only if Omar can show that the disclosure caused him financial harm.
Yes, because information relating to the representation stays protected even if it has become public.
No, because Tess was speaking socially to a friend and not in connection with any legal matter.
oe: Rule 1.6(a) is broader than privilege; it doesn't depend on secrecy. Even "generally known" former-client information may be used under Rule 1.9(c)(1), not revealed.
Confidentiality survives the end of the relationship. Rule 1.9(c)(2) forbids revealing a former client's information except as the Rules permit.
Discipline under Rule 1.6(a) doesn't require harm to the client; the unauthorized revelation is the violation.

Correct. Rule 1.6(a) covers all "information relating to the representation of a client," whatever its source, and the duty continues after the representation ends (Rule 1.9(c)). Public availability doesn't remove the protection; Rule 1.9(c)(1) allows only use, not disclosure, of information that has become generally known.
The duty doesn't depend on the setting of the disclosure. Casual conversation is a common way lawyers violate Rule 1.6(a).
questions.e: Rule 1.6(a) protects all information relating to the representation, from any source and even if public; it continues after the representation (Rule 1.9(c)), and only Rule 1.9(c)(1) allows use, not disclosure, of generally known former-client information.

questions.q: Lawyer Mia works on client matters from coffee shops. She regularly joins the shop's open public Wi-Fi without any security measures, leaves her laptop unlocked and open when she goes to the counter, and has never used the firm's encrypted connection. No client information has yet been seen or taken. Is Mia subject to discipline?
o: No, because no client information has actually been disclosed to anyone.
Yes, because she has not made reasonable efforts to prevent unauthorized access to client information.
No, because lawyers are not required to understand technology to practice competently.
Yes, because any unauthorized access to client information is automatically a violation of Rule 1.6.
No, because only the firm's managing partners are responsible for the firm's data security.
oe: Rule 1.6(c) is a duty of reasonable precautions, not a guarantee against loss. Unreasonable practices violate it whether or not a disclosure has happened yet.

Correct. Rule 1.6(c) requires a lawyer to "make reasonable efforts to prevent the inadvertent or unauthorized disclosure of, or unauthorized access to, information relating to the representation." The duty is breached by unreasonable practices, even before a breach occurs; Rule 1.6, Comment [18] lists the factors.
Rule 1.1, Comment [8] says competence includes keeping abreast of the benefits and risks of relevant technology, and Rule 1.6(c) requires reasonable safeguards.
Rule 1.6, Comment [18] says unauthorized access or disclosure does not violate Rule 1.6(c) if the lawyer made reasonable efforts to prevent it. The violation here is the lack of reasonable efforts.
Managers have their own duties under Rule 5.1(a), but each lawyer must take reasonable care with client information under Rule 1.6(c).
questions.e: Rule 1.6(c) requires reasonable efforts to prevent inadvertent or unauthorized disclosure of, or access to, client information; Comment [18] weighs factors such as the sensitivity of the information, the likelihood of disclosure, and the cost and difficulty of safeguards.

questions.q: Lawyer Vince met with Client Felix a week before Felix died, and Felix discussed matters related to a federal investigation. A grand jury now subpoenas Vince's notes of the meeting, arguing that the attorney-client privilege ended at Felix's death and that the notes are needed in a criminal case. What is the most likely result?
o: The notes are privileged, because the attorney-client privilege generally survives the client's death.
The notes must be produced, because the privilege ends when the client dies.
The notes must be produced, because the privilege yields whenever the information is important to a criminal case.
The notes are protected only by the duty of confidentiality, which a subpoena overrides under Rule 1.6(b)(6).
The notes are protected, but only if Felix's estate formally asserts the privilege within 30 days of death.
oe: Correct. In Swidler & Berlin v. United States, the Supreme Court held that the attorney-client privilege survives the client's death, even in a criminal investigation, because clients might not speak candidly if they feared disclosure after death.
Swidler & Berlin rejected that argument; the privilege continues after death.
Swidler & Berlin refused to create a balancing exception for criminal cases; posthumous needs don't defeat the privilege.
Rule 1.6(b)(6) permits disclosure to comply with a court order, but the privilege is an evidentiary rule that lets the lawyer resist the subpoena in the first place. Both protections apply here.
No such deadline exists; the lawyer may and should assert the privilege on the client's behalf.
questions.e: The attorney-client privilege (an evidentiary rule protecting confidential lawyer-client communications for legal advice) survives the client's death (Swidler & Berlin); the Rule 1.6 duty of confidentiality is broader and applies everywhere, not just in court.

questions.tag: MR 1.6(b)(1): reasonably certain death or substantial bodily harm
questions.q: During a meeting about her divorce, Client Cora tells Lawyer Lyn that her estranged husband keeps a loaded gun at home and "means it" when he threatens to kill their neighbor over a fence dispute; she says the husband told her he would do it this weekend. Cora begs Lyn not to tell anyone. May Lyn reveal the threat to the police?
o: No, because the threat came from the husband, not the client, so the exception does not apply.
Yes, and she must, because the Model Rules require a lawyer to disclose information to prevent a death.
No, unless the threatened harm would result from a crime in which Cora used Lyn's services.
Yes, but only after Lyn withdraws from Cora's divorce case, so that she no longer owes Cora a duty.
Yes, to the extent reasonably necessary to prevent reasonably certain death or substantial bodily harm.
oe: Rule 1.6(b)(1) is not limited to harm threatened by the client. Comment [6] makes clear it protects life regardless of who threatens it.
Rule 1.6(b) is permissive: "may." Rule 1.6, Comment [17] says a lawyer's decision not to disclose as permitted does not violate the Rule.
That limit belongs to the financial-harm exceptions, Rule 1.6(b)(2) and (3). The bodily-harm exception has no crime or use-of-services requirement.
Nothing in Rule 1.6(b)(1) requires withdrawal before disclosure; the lawyer may reveal what is reasonably necessary while continuing the representation.

Correct. Rule 1.6(b)(1) permits disclosure "to prevent reasonably certain death or substantial bodily harm." The exception does not require that the client be the wrongdoer or that a crime be involved; Comment [6] says harm is reasonably certain if it will be suffered imminently or there is a present and substantial threat.
questions.e: Rule 1.6(b)(1) permits (never requires) revealing information to the extent reasonably necessary to prevent reasonably certain death or substantial bodily harm, from any source; Rule 1.6, Comment [6] defines "reasonably certain."

questions.tag: MR 1.6(b)(2)–(3): client used the lawyer's services
questions.q: Lawyer Hugo prepared offering documents for Client Kurt's investment fund. After the investors have paid in, Hugo learns that Kurt lied to him about the fund's assets, so the documents Hugo drafted were false, and that Kurt has spent part of the investors' money. Kurt refuses to correct anything. Which statement best describes what Hugo may do?
o: Nothing, because the fraud is already complete and the exceptions apply only to prevent future harm.
Reveal what is reasonably necessary to mitigate or rectify the investors' loss, since Kurt used his services.
Reveal the fraud, and he must do so, because a lawyer is required to rectify a client fraud that used his services.
Reveal the fraud only if the investors' losses threaten someone's physical safety.
Reveal the fraud to anyone he chooses, in as much detail as he wishes, because Kurt forfeited confidentiality.
oe: Rule 1.6(b)(3) expressly covers mitigating or rectifying injury that has already resulted, so long as the client used the lawyer's services.

Correct. Rule 1.6(b)(3) permits disclosure to prevent, mitigate or rectify substantial financial injury that "has resulted from the client's commission of a crime or fraud in furtherance of which the client has used the lawyer's services." Because the fraud is complete, (b)(3) rather than (b)(2) fits, and Hugo should also consider withdrawal and disaffirming his work.
Rule 1.6(b)(3) is permissive. Mandatory disclosure arises in other settings, such as Rule 3.3 before a tribunal, not here.
That is the bodily-harm exception, Rule 1.6(b)(1). Financial injury is covered separately by Rule 1.6(b)(2) and (3).
Disclosure under any Rule 1.6(b) exception is limited to what the lawyer reasonably believes necessary (Rule 1.6, Comment [16]).
questions.e: Rule 1.6(b)(2) (prevent) and (b)(3) (prevent, mitigate or rectify) permit disclosure of a client crime or fraud reasonably certain to cause, or that has caused, substantial financial injury, but only when the client used the lawyer's services; disclosure must be limited to what is reasonably necessary.

questions.q: Client Ida refuses to pay Lawyer Abe's final $18,000 invoice in a custody case, claiming Abe did little work. Abe sues Ida for the fee. To prove the value of his work, he wants to describe in his complaint the hours spent on specific motions and the facts of Ida's case those motions involved. Ida objects that this reveals her confidential information. May Abe include it?
o: No, because a lawyer may never use a client's confidential information against the client.
Yes, to the extent he reasonably believes necessary to establish his claim for the fee.
Yes, and he may include any information about Ida that might pressure her to settle.
No, unless Ida first files a disciplinary complaint against him.
Yes, but only if he first obtains a court order permitting the disclosure.
oe: Rule 1.6(b)(5) is an express exception for controversies between lawyer and client, including fee disputes.

Correct. Rule 1.6(b)(5) permits disclosure "to establish a claim or defense on behalf of the lawyer in a controversy between the lawyer and the client." Comment [11] confirms a lawyer may prove services rendered in an action to collect a fee, but Comment [16] limits disclosure to what is reasonably necessary.
Disclosure under Rule 1.6(b)(5) is limited to what is reasonably necessary to establish the claim; using confidences as leverage would violate Rule 1.6 and possibly Rule 8.4(c).
Rule 1.6(b)(5) covers the lawyer's own claim against the client; it does not wait for the client to accuse the lawyer.
A court order is a separate exception, Rule 1.6(b)(6). The claim-or-defense exception needs no order, though Comment [16] suggests protective measures such as sealing where possible.
questions.e: Rule 1.6(b)(5) permits disclosure reasonably necessary to establish a claim or defense in a controversy between lawyer and client (such as a fee suit), to defend against charges based on conduct involving the client, or to respond to allegations about the representation.

questions.area: When Disclosure Becomes Mandatory; Hard Cases
questions.q: Lawyer Wren represents Client Xavier in two matters. In a pending court case, Xavier gave a sworn answer to an interrogatory that Wren now knows was false. In a separate private negotiation, Xavier earlier misstated a fact to the other side, without using Wren's services, and the negotiation has ended. Xavier refuses to correct either. Which statement is correct?
o: Wren must disclose both misstatements, because a lawyer may never let a client's false statement stand.
Wren must remedy the false court answer, even by revealing confidences, but may not reveal the negotiation lie.
Wren may not disclose either misstatement, because Rule 1.6 protects all information about the client's conduct.
Wren must disclose the negotiation misstatement to the other side, but may only withdraw from the court case.
Wren may disclose the court misstatement, but only if Xavier used Wren's services to give the false answer.
oe: Only the tribunal setting makes disclosure mandatory over Rule 1.6. In the negotiation, Rule 4.1(b) defers to Rule 1.6, which forbids disclosure here.

Correct. Rule 3.3(a)(3) and (c) require reasonable remedial measures, including disclosure to the tribunal if necessary, "even if compliance requires disclosure of information otherwise protected by Rule 1.6." Outside a tribunal, Rule 4.1(b) requires disclosure only when Rule 1.6 permits it, and no Rule 1.6(b) exception covers a completed fraud that didn't use Wren's services.
Rule 3.3(c) expressly overrides Rule 1.6 for false evidence offered before a tribunal.
This reverses the rules. The duty to the tribunal is the mandatory one; withdrawal alone may not cure false evidence already offered (Rule 3.3, Comment [10]).
The use-of-services limit belongs to Rule 1.6(b)(2) and (3). Rule 3.3(a)(3) applies to any material false evidence the lawyer knows the client offered.
questions.e: Disclosure is mandatory over Rule 1.6 only in narrow settings, chiefly Rule 3.3(c) (false evidence or fraud before a tribunal); Rule 4.1(b)'s duty to disclose to third parties applies only when Rule 1.6 permits disclosure.

questions.tag: Duty of loyalty: taking the client's opportunity
questions.q: Lawyer Gil represents Client Rhea in negotiating to buy a vacant lot for her restaurant. During the talks Gil learns that the seller would accept far less than Rhea has offered. Without telling Rhea, Gil buys the lot himself through his own company at the lower price, planning to lease it to Rhea at a fair rent. Which statement best describes Gil's conduct?
o: It was proper, because Gil plans to lease the lot to Rhea at a fair rent, so she suffers no harm.
It breached only his duty of care, because he negotiated carelessly for Rhea.
It was proper, because a lawyer may use information learned in a representation so long as he doesn't reveal it.
It breached his duty of loyalty, because a fiduciary may not take his client's opportunity.
It breached only his duty of candor, which he could have cured by telling Rhea after the purchase closed.
oe: Loyalty is breached by self-dealing whether or not the beneficiary is harmed; the fairness of the later lease doesn't cure taking her opportunity.
The problem isn't careless work but self-interest: Gil used his position to benefit himself at Rhea's expense, which is loyalty.
Rule 1.8(b) forbids using information relating to the representation to the client's disadvantage without informed consent, even without revealing it.

Correct. Loyalty is the core fiduciary duty: a lawyer must put the client's interests in the engagement ahead of his own (Meinhard's "punctilio of an honor the most sensitive"). Using information from the representation to take the client's deal also violates Rule 1.8(b), and the purchase is adverse to the client under Rule 1.8(a).
He also failed to keep Rhea informed under Rule 1.4, but disclosure after the fact doesn't cure the self-dealing. Loyalty is the primary breach.
questions.e: The four fiduciary duties (loyalty, care, confidentiality, candor) are analyzed separately; loyalty forbids self-dealing and taking the client's opportunities (Meinhard), and the Rules enforce it in Rule 1.8(a) and (b).

questions.tag: MR 1.8(j): sexual relations with a client
questions.q: Lawyer Kendall begins representing Client Jordan in a contract dispute. Two months into the case, the two begin a consensual romantic and sexual relationship. Kendall believes the relationship won't affect her work, and Jordan, an experienced businessperson, insists it is his choice. Is Kendall subject to discipline?
o: No, because the relationship is consensual and Jordan is a sophisticated adult.
Yes, because a lawyer may not begin sexual relations with a current client, whether or not the client consents.
No, unless the relationship actually harms Kendall's representation of Jordan.
Yes, unless Jordan gives informed consent, confirmed in writing, after advice to consult independent counsel.
No, because Rule 1.8(j) applies only in family-law and criminal matters, where clients are vulnerable.
oe: Rule 1.8(j) applies even when the relationship is consensual and the client is sophisticated; consent is not a defense.

Correct. Rule 1.8(j) forbids sexual relations with a client "unless a consensual sexual relationship existed between them when the client-lawyer relationship commenced." The relationship began during the representation, and Rule 1.8, Comment [20] makes the prohibition apply regardless of consent or prejudice.
Rule 1.8(j) is a flat prohibition; Rule 1.8, Comment [20] says it applies regardless of whether the relationship is consensual and regardless of the absence of prejudice to the client.
Rule 1.8(j) is not consentable. The written-consent procedure belongs to other rules, such as Rule 1.8(a).
Rule 1.8(j) applies to all clients in all kinds of matters.
questions.e: Rule 1.8(j) bars sexual relations with a client unless a consensual relationship predated the representation; consent and lack of prejudice are no defense, and under Rule 1.8(k) the ban is personal, not imputed.

questions.q: Lawyer Pam represents Client Quinn, a plaintiff in a personal-injury case. Quinn told Pam at the outset that she wanted to go to trial "to make a point." The defense now offers $150,000, which Pam thinks is too low and which she is sure Quinn would reject. Pam rejects the offer without telling Quinn. Is Pam subject to discipline?
o: No, because Quinn said she wanted to go to trial, which authorized Pam to reject any offer.
No, because Pam reasonably believed the offer was too low, and the means of the case are for the lawyer to decide.
Yes, but only if a court later finds that Quinn would have accepted the offer.
No, because a lawyer must communicate only written offers, and the rule does not reach oral ones.
Yes, because a lawyer must promptly tell the client of a settlement offer like this one.
oe: A general preference for trial is not a decision about a specific offer. Comment [2]'s exception applies only when the client has indicated that an offer of that kind is acceptable or unacceptable.
Whether to settle is an objective reserved to the client under Rule 1.2(a), not a matter of means.
Discipline doesn't depend on proving what the client would have done; the failure to communicate is the violation of Rule 1.4(a)(1).
Rule 1.4 makes no distinction between oral and written offers.

Correct. Rule 1.4(a)(1) requires prompt communication of any decision requiring the client's informed consent, and Rule 1.4, Comment [2] says a lawyer who receives a settlement offer must promptly inform the client unless the client has previously indicated the offer would be acceptable or unacceptable. Quinn's general wish for a trial did not address this offer. Whether to settle is Quinn's call under Rule 1.2(a).
questions.e: Settlement and plea offers must be promptly communicated (Rule 1.4(a)(1), Comment [2]) unless the client has already said whether such an offer is acceptable; the decision to settle belongs to the client (Rule 1.2(a)).

questions.q: Lawyer Saul represents Client Teo in a fraud case. Saul learns that his own missed deadline caused the court to strike Teo's best defense. Saul fears Teo will fire him and report him, so he decides to say nothing until the case is over and to try to make up the ground at trial. Is Saul's plan proper?
o: Yes, because Rule 1.4, Comment [7] permits a lawyer to delay transmitting information that would upset the client.
No, because a lawyer may not withhold information to serve his own interests, and must tell the client about a material error.
Yes, because a lawyer has no duty to report his own mistakes so long as he continues to work diligently on the case.
No, but only because Saul's error must also be reported to the disciplinary authority under Rule 8.3.
Yes, if Saul's malpractice insurer instructs him not to discuss the error with the client.
oe: Comment [7] permits delay when the client would likely react imprudently, and expressly bars withholding information to serve the lawyer's own interest or convenience.

Correct. Rule 1.4(a)(3) and (b) require keeping the client reasonably informed and explaining matters enough for informed decisions. Rule 1.4, Comment [7] allows delay only to protect the client (for example, from an imprudent reaction), never to serve the lawyer's own interest or convenience. A material error the client needs to know about must be disclosed.
The duty of candor includes telling the client about material developments, including the lawyer's own errors, so the client can decide whether to keep the lawyer or seek advice.
Rule 8.3 concerns reporting another lawyer's misconduct. The issue here is Saul's own duty to communicate under Rule 1.4.
An insurer's wishes don't override the lawyer's duty to the client under Rule 1.4.
questions.e: Rule 1.4 requires keeping the client reasonably informed and explaining matters enough to permit informed decisions; Comment [7] allows only protective delay, never withholding to serve the lawyer, so a lawyer must tell the client about a material error.

questions.area: The Lawyer as Agent: Authority (Ch. 6; MR 1.2(a))
questions.tag: MR 1.2(a): blanket settlement authority; apparent authority
questions.q: Client Lara hires Lawyer Moe to pursue an employment claim. Moe has never discussed settlement numbers with her. At a mediation Lara could not attend, Moe accepts the employer's $60,000 offer, telling the employer's counsel, "I'm her lawyer, I can settle." Lara refuses to sign. Is the settlement binding on Lara?
o: Yes, because a lawyer has implied authority to settle any claim he has been hired to pursue.
No, because retaining a lawyer does not by itself give the lawyer authority to settle the client's claim.
Yes, because the employer's counsel reasonably relied on Moe's statement that he had authority.
No, but only because a settlement must be approved by the court before it binds the parties.
Yes, unless Lara can prove that $60,000 was an unreasonably low amount for her claim.
oe: Settlement is an objective reserved to the client under Rule 1.2(a), so it can't be implied from the retention itself.

Correct. Whether to settle is reserved to the client (Rule 1.2(a)). Moe had no actual authority, and hiring a lawyer alone creates no apparent authority to settle; a lawyer's own assertions of authority don't count, because apparent authority must be traceable to the principal's manifestations.
Apparent authority depends on the principal's manifestations to the third party, not the agent's own claims. Lara said nothing to the employer.
Most private settlements need no court approval; the problem is Moe's lack of authority.
The reasonableness of the amount doesn't matter. Without authority or ratification, the client isn't bound.
questions.e: Rule 1.2(a) reserves the decision to settle to the client; a lawyer needs actual authority (or the client's ratification) to settle, and mere retention or the lawyer's own word creates no apparent authority.

questions.area: The Lawyer as Agent: Authority (Ch. 6; MR 1.2(a))
questions.tag: MR 1.2(a): client's reserved decisions in a criminal case
questions.q: Defense lawyer Bea strongly believes her client Cy should waive a jury and try his case to the judge, who is known to be skeptical of the police witnesses. Cy insists on a jury. Bea also wants to call an expert whose testimony Cy thinks is unnecessary. Which of these decisions are for Cy to make?
o: Both decisions, because the client controls every decision in a criminal case.
Neither decision, because both are trial tactics that belong to defense counsel.
The expert only, because the client pays for the expert and so controls whether to hire one.
The jury waiver only, because the choice of witnesses is a matter of means for the lawyer after consultation.
The jury waiver only, but Bea may override Cy if she reasonably believes a bench trial is in his best interest.
oe: The client controls the objectives and the decisions Rule 1.2(a) reserves; technical and tactical matters, such as which witnesses to call, are ordinarily for the lawyer after consultation.
Waiving a jury is one of the decisions Rule 1.2(a) reserves to the criminal client.
Payment doesn't move a tactical decision to the client; and the jury waiver is the reserved decision.

Correct. Rule 1.2(a) says that in a criminal case the client decides, after consultation, whether to waive a jury trial, the plea, and whether to testify. Which witnesses to call is a tactical means decision that the lawyer makes after consulting the client (Rule 1.2, Comment [2]; Rule 1.4(a)(2)).
Bea may advise, but she may not override Cy on a decision Rule 1.2(a) reserves to him.
questions.e: Rule 1.2(a): the client decides objectives and, in a criminal case, the plea, jury waiver and whether to testify; the lawyer handles means, after consulting under Rule 1.4(a)(2).

questions.q: Lawyer Ray agrees to represent Client Sue in a car-accident claim for one-third of any recovery. He explains the terms clearly in a meeting and sends Sue a letter summarizing them, but Sue never signs anything. The letter does not say whether litigation expenses will be deducted before or after the one-third is calculated. Which statement is correct?
o: Ray complied with the Rules, because the fee terms were communicated to Sue in writing.
Ray violated Rule 1.5(c), but only because a one-third contingent fee in a car-accident case is unreasonable.
Ray complied with the Rules, because Rule 1.5(b) says only that fee terms should "preferably" be in writing.
Ray violated Rule 1.5(c) only if he fails to give Sue a written closing statement at the end of the case.
Ray violated Rule 1.5(c), because a contingent fee needs a signed writing that explains expenses.
oe: A writing that the lawyer sends is enough for an hourly or flat fee under Rule 1.5(b), not for a contingent fee, which Rule 1.5(c) requires the client to sign.
A one-third contingency in a personal-injury case is common and not unreasonable on its face under Rule 1.5(a). The violation is the missing signed writing and expense terms.
"Preferably in writing" is Rule 1.5(b)'s general rule; Rule 1.5(c) imposes stricter requirements for contingent fees.
The closing statement is a separate Rule 1.5(c) requirement. The agreement itself must also be in a signed writing with the required terms.

Correct. Rule 1.5(c) requires a contingent-fee agreement to be "in a writing signed by the client" stating the method of determining the fee, including the percentages, the litigation and other expenses to be deducted, and whether they are deducted before or after the fee is calculated.
questions.e: Rule 1.5(c): a contingent fee agreement must be in a writing signed by the client stating the method of calculating the fee, the expenses to be deducted and whether before or after the fee is calculated, and the client's liability for expenses; at the end the lawyer gives a written statement of the outcome and the remittance.

questions.q: Lawyer Nell has represented Client Orbit Corp. for six years at an hourly rate of $350. Orbit asks Nell to handle a new lease negotiation, and she agrees, intending to charge the same $350 rate. She sends no engagement letter and says nothing about the fee. Is Nell subject to discipline?
o: Yes, because Rule 1.5(b) requires a written fee agreement for every new matter.
Yes, because she must obtain Orbit's informed consent, confirmed in writing, to her hourly rate.
No, because fee communications are required only in contingent-fee matters.
No, because she is charging a regularly represented client on the same basis.
Yes, unless Nell's hourly rate has been approved by a court as reasonable.
oe: Rule 1.5(b) says "preferably in writing," and it exempts regularly represented clients charged on the same basis or rate.
Fee terms need only be communicated under Rule 1.5(b); no informed consent confirmed in writing is required for an ordinary hourly fee.
Rule 1.5(b) applies to all fees, except for the regularly-represented-client situation. Contingent fees have additional writing requirements under Rule 1.5(c).

Correct. Rule 1.5(b) requires communicating the scope and the basis or rate of the fee, preferably in writing, "except when the lawyer will charge a regularly represented client on the same basis or rate."
No court approval is required for a fee; reasonableness under Rule 1.5(a) is judged by its factors.
questions.e: Rule 1.5(b): communicate the scope of the representation and the basis or rate of the fee and expenses, preferably in writing, before or within a reasonable time after starting, except for a regularly represented client charged on the same basis; any changes must also be communicated.

questions.area: Limits on Fees, Retainers, and Fee Sharing (MR 1.5(a), (d), (e); 5.4; 7.2(b))
questions.q: Client Dee asks Lawyer Ed to represent her in her divorce. She has little cash, so Ed proposes a fee of 20 percent of whatever property settlement and alimony he obtains for her. Dee agrees in a signed writing. Is the fee arrangement proper?
o: Yes, because Dee consented in a signed writing, as Rule 1.5(c) requires for contingent fees.
No, because a fee contingent on the amount of alimony or a property settlement in a divorce is prohibited.
Yes, because 20 percent is a reasonable fee in light of Dee's inability to pay hourly rates.
No, because contingent fees are prohibited in all civil cases that do not involve personal injury.
Yes, so long as the fee is not contingent on securing the divorce itself.
oe: A signed writing satisfies the form requirements of Rule 1.5(c), but Rule 1.5(d) makes this kind of fee substantively prohibited, consent or not.

Correct. Rule 1.5(d)(1) forbids a fee in a domestic relations matter "the payment or amount of which is contingent upon the securing of a divorce or upon the amount of alimony or support, or property settlement in lieu thereof." Client consent doesn't cure it.
Reasonableness under Rule 1.5(a) is irrelevant when Rule 1.5(d)(1) prohibits the arrangement altogether.
Contingent fees are allowed in most civil matters. Rule 1.5(d) singles out domestic relations matters and criminal cases.
Rule 1.5(d)(1) also bars fees contingent on the amount of alimony, support or a property settlement in lieu of them.
questions.e: Rule 1.5(d) prohibits contingent fees (1) in domestic relations matters contingent on securing a divorce or on the amount of alimony, support or property settlement, and (2) for representing a defendant in a criminal case; Comment [6] allows contingent fees to collect past-due support.

questions.area: Limits on Fees, Retainers, and Fee Sharing (MR 1.5(a), (d), (e); 5.4; 7.2(b))
questions.tag: MR 1.5(e): dividing fees with a lawyer in another firm
questions.q: Lawyer Fay refers a medical-malpractice client to Lawyer Gus, a specialist in another firm. Fay will do no further work on the case. Gus agrees to pay Fay one-third of his contingent fee. The client is told that the two lawyers will share the fee but is never told what share Fay will get, and nothing is put in writing to the client. Fay does not assume any responsibility for the representation. Is the fee division proper?
o: No, because Fay did no work, took no responsibility, and the client never agreed in writing to her share.
Yes, because the client knew the lawyers would share the fee and the total fee is reasonable.
Yes, because a referring lawyer may always receive a reasonable referral fee from the lawyer who handles the case.
No, because lawyers who practice in different firms may never divide a fee, even with the client's written consent.
No, but it would be proper if Fay gave the client's informed consent form to Gus to keep in his file.
oe: Correct. Rule 1.5(e) allows a division between lawyers not in the same firm only if (1) it is in proportion to the services each performs or each assumes joint responsibility, (2) the client agrees to the arrangement, including each lawyer's share, and the agreement is confirmed in writing, and (3) the total fee is reasonable.
Knowledge of sharing isn't enough. Rule 1.5(e)(2) requires the client's agreement to each lawyer's share, confirmed in writing, and Rule 1.5(e)(1) isn't met either.
A pure referral fee without proportional work or joint responsibility violates Rule 1.5(e)(1), and paying for a recommendation is barred by Rule 7.2(b).
Rule 1.5(e) expressly permits divisions between lawyers not in the same firm when its conditions are met.
The issue isn't record keeping; Fay must either work in proportion or assume joint responsibility, and the client must agree to each share, confirmed in writing.
questions.e: Rule 1.5(e): lawyers in different firms may divide a fee only if (all required) (1) the division is proportional to services or each assumes joint responsibility, (2) the client agrees, including the share each gets, confirmed in writing, and (3) the total fee is reasonable.

questions.area: Limits on Fees, Retainers, and Fee Sharing (MR 1.5(a), (d), (e); 5.4; 7.2(b))
questions.q: Lawyer Hal requires a $15,000 "nonrefundable retainer" from each new criminal defense client, deposits it in his operating account, and treats it as earned on receipt, though it is meant to pay for his hourly work on the case. Client Ivy pays it and fires Hal two weeks later, after he has done $2,000 worth of work. Hal refuses to return anything. Which statement best describes Hal's conduct?
o: He must refund the unearned $13,000, because a fee paid in advance for future services belongs to the client until earned.
He may keep all of it, because Ivy agreed in advance that the retainer was nonrefundable.
He may keep all of it, because a retainer compensates a lawyer for being available and turning away other clients.
He must refund all $15,000, because Ivy fired him before the case ended.
He violated the Rules only by depositing the money in his operating account; once it is there, he need not refund it.
oe: Correct. A payment for future services is an advance fee deposit, not a true retainer for availability. Rule 1.15(c) requires depositing it in trust and withdrawing only as earned, and Rule 1.16(d) requires refunding the unearned part on termination. Labeling it "nonrefundable" doesn't make an unreasonable fee reasonable under Rule 1.5(a).
A label cannot convert an advance payment for services into an earned fee; keeping it after $2,000 of work would be an unreasonable fee under Rule 1.5(a) and violate Rule 1.16(d).
That describes a true (general) retainer. Hal's payment was meant to pay for his hourly work on the case, so it is an advance fee deposit.
Hal is entitled to the reasonable value of the work he did; only the unearned portion must be refunded.
Depositing it in his own account also violated Rule 1.15(c), but the duty to refund the unearned portion under Rule 1.16(d) remains.
questions.e: A true retainer pays for availability and may be earned on receipt if reasonable; an advance fee for future services must go into trust (Rule 1.15(c)) and its unearned part must be refunded on termination (Rule 1.16(d)), whatever it is called.

questions.q: Lawyer Jo settles Client Kai's personal-injury case for $90,000 and deposits the check in her trust account. Under the fee agreement, Jo's fee is $30,000. Kai now claims the fee should be only $20,000. No one else claims any of the money. What should Jo do?
o: Hold the entire $90,000 in the trust account until she and Kai resolve their dispute over the fee.
Pay herself $30,000, because her fee agreement entitles her to that amount, and pay Kai the rest.
Pay the undisputed $60,000 to Kai and $20,000 to herself, and hold the disputed $10,000 in trust.
Pay Kai the full $90,000 and sue him for her fee.
Move the disputed $10,000 into her operating account for safekeeping until the dispute ends.
oe: Rule 1.15(e) requires prompt distribution of the undisputed portions; holding everything would coerce the client.
The $10,000 difference is disputed. Rule 1.15(e) bars paying disputed funds to either claimant until the dispute is resolved.

Correct. Rule 1.15(e) requires a lawyer to keep separate any funds in which two or more persons claim interests until the dispute is resolved, and to promptly distribute all portions not in dispute. Rule 1.15, Comment [3] says the lawyer may not hold the undisputed funds to coerce the client.
Jo may withdraw the undisputed part of her fee; she need not, and should not, give the client funds that belong to her. Only the disputed amount stays in trust.
Disputed funds must stay in the trust account; moving them to an operating account is commingling and conversion under Rule 1.15(a).
questions.e: Rule 1.15(e): when the lawyer and the client (or a third party) both claim funds, keep the disputed portion in trust until the dispute is resolved and promptly distribute the undisputed portions (Rule 1.15, Comment [3]).

questions.tag: MR 1.15(a)–(b): commingling and the bank-charge exception
questions.q: Lawyer Lev keeps $3,000 of his own money in his client trust account. He explains that his bank charges about $40 a month in fees on the account and that he likes a "cushion" so that he never accidentally overdraws a client's balance. Is Lev subject to discipline under the Model Rules?
o: Yes, because a lawyer may keep only enough of his own money in trust to pay bank service charges.
No, because his purpose of protecting clients' balances is a legitimate one.
No, because a lawyer may keep any amount of his own money in trust so long as he keeps accurate records.
Yes, because a lawyer may never deposit any of his own money in a client trust account.
No, because commingling is a violation only if a client's money is actually lost.
oe: Correct. Rule 1.15(b) allows a lawyer to deposit his own funds in a trust account "for the sole purpose of paying bank service charges on that account, but only in an amount necessary for that purpose." A $3,000 cushion is commingling, forbidden by Rule 1.15(a). (Delaware's Rule 1.15 caps the bank-charge amount at $2,000, so Lev's cushion would fail there too.)
Good motives don't permit commingling. Rule 1.15(b) allows only the amount needed for bank charges.
Accurate records are required, but they don't permit commingling; Rule 1.15(a) requires the lawyer's property to be kept separate.
Too strong. Rule 1.15(b) permits a lawyer's own funds in the amount necessary to pay bank service charges.
