Commingling violates Rule 1.15(a) whether or not any client suffers a loss.
questions.e: Rule 1.15(a) requires client and third-party property to be kept separate from the lawyer's; Rule 1.15(b) permits only enough of the lawyer's own funds to pay bank charges (Delaware caps it at $2,000), and records must be kept for five years.

questions.tag: MR 1.8(a): business transaction with a client
questions.q: Lawyer Mona has represented Client Ned's landscaping company for years. Ned offers Mona a 10 percent stake in his new venture in exchange for her doing the venture's legal work at half her usual rate. The terms are fair to Ned. Mona explains the terms in a detailed email, and Ned replies "Sounds great, let's do it." Mona never suggests that Ned talk to another lawyer about the deal. Is Mona subject to discipline?
o: No, because the terms were fair and reasonable to Ned and fully disclosed to him in writing.
No, because accepting stock in a client's business in exchange for legal work is a fee arrangement governed only by Rule 1.5.
Yes, because a lawyer may never acquire an ownership interest in a client's business.
No, because Ned's reply email was informed consent confirmed in writing.
Yes, because she did not advise Ned in writing to seek independent counsel or get his signed consent.
oe: Fairness and written disclosure are only Rule 1.8(a)(1). Mona also needed written advice to seek independent counsel and a consent signed by the client.
Rule 1.8, Comment [1] says Rule 1.8(a) applies when a lawyer accepts an interest in the client's business as payment, in addition to Rule 1.5.
Rule 1.8(a) permits such transactions if its three requirements are met; it is not a flat ban.
Rule 1.8(a)(3) requires more than "confirmed in writing": a writing signed by the client consenting to the essential terms and the lawyer's role.

Correct. Rule 1.8(a) requires (all required): (1) fair and reasonable terms fully disclosed in writing; (2) written advice of the desirability of seeking independent counsel and a reasonable opportunity to do so; and (3) the client's informed consent, in a writing signed by the client, to the essential terms and the lawyer's role. Fair terms and an email exchange satisfy only the first.
questions.e: Rule 1.8(a): a business transaction with a client or acquisition of an interest adverse to the client requires (all required) (1) fair, fully disclosed terms in writing, (2) written advice to seek independent counsel and a reasonable chance to do so, and (3) the client's informed consent in a signed writing.

questions.tag: MR 1.8(e): financial assistance and its exceptions
questions.q: Lawyer Otto represents Client Pia, who cannot work because of the injuries at issue in her personal-injury suit, on a contingent fee. Pia is about to be evicted. Which of the following may Otto do?
o: Advance the costs of her expert witnesses, with repayment contingent on the outcome of the case.
Lend her two months' rent, to be repaid from her recovery, so she can stay housed while the case goes on.
Give her a modest gift for rent, because the Rules allow humanitarian gifts to indigent clients.
Guarantee her landlord that the rent will be paid from any settlement.
Pay her medical bills, so long as she agrees to reimburse him if she wins.
oe: Correct. Rule 1.8(e)(1) lets a lawyer advance court costs and expenses of litigation, with repayment contingent on the outcome. Paying her living expenses is barred here; the humanitarian exception in Rule 1.8(e)(3) applies only to indigent clients represented pro bono, and Otto is working on a contingent fee.
A loan for living expenses in connection with pending litigation is financial assistance forbidden by Rule 1.8(e); repayment from the recovery doesn't save it.
Rule 1.8(e)(3) allows modest gifts for basic living expenses only when the lawyer represents the indigent client pro bono, not on a contingent fee.
Guaranteeing a client's debts in connection with pending litigation is financial assistance forbidden by Rule 1.8(e).
Medical bills are living expenses, not litigation expenses; Rule 1.8(e) forbids paying them whether or not repayment is promised.
questions.e: Rule 1.8(e) bars financial assistance to a client in pending or contemplated litigation except (1) advancing court costs and litigation expenses (repayment may be contingent), (2) paying them for an indigent client, and (3) modest gifts for basic living expenses to an indigent client represented pro bono.

questions.tag: MR 1.8(c): drafting a will that leaves the lawyer a gift
questions.q: Client Edna, a longtime friend but not a relative of Lawyer Fritz, asks him to draft her will and to include a $100,000 bequest to Fritz in gratitude for years of help. Fritz drafts the will as she asks. Is Fritz subject to discipline?
o: No, because the bequest was Edna's idea, and Fritz did not solicit it.
No, because a long friendship counts as a close relationship that the Rule exempts.
Yes, because he drafted an instrument giving himself a substantial gift.
No, if Fritz obtains Edna's informed consent, confirmed in writing, to the gift.
Yes, because a lawyer may never accept any gift from a client.
oe: Not soliciting the gift avoids one part of Rule 1.8(c), but preparing the instrument that makes the substantial gift is separately forbidden.
Rule 1.8(c) exempts only gifts from related persons: a spouse, child, grandchild, parent, grandparent or other relative or individual with a close familial relationship. Friendship is not enough.

Correct. Rule 1.8(c) forbids a lawyer to "prepare on behalf of a client an instrument giving the lawyer or a person related to the lawyer any substantial gift unless the lawyer or other recipient of the gift is related to the client." Edna's wishes don't cure it; she should use another lawyer to draft that gift (Rule 1.8, Comment [7]).
Rule 1.8(c) is not cured by consent; the lawyer simply may not prepare such an instrument for an unrelated client.

Too broad. Rule 1.8, Comment [6] says a lawyer may accept a gift from a client if the transaction meets general standards of fairness; small gifts are fine. The problem is soliciting or drafting a substantial gift.
questions.e: Rule 1.8(c): a lawyer may not solicit a substantial gift from a client, or prepare an instrument giving the lawyer or a relative a substantial gift, unless the recipient is related to the client; accepting an unsolicited gift is governed by general fairness (Comment [6]).

questions.q: Parent Pat hires Lawyer Quill to defend Pat's 22-year-old son Rob against a drug charge and pays the full fee. Pat tells Quill, "I'm paying, so I want weekly reports on everything Rob tells you, and I'll decide whether he takes a plea." Rob agrees to Quill's representation but not to sharing information with Pat. What must Quill do?
o: Follow Pat's instructions, because a person who pays the lawyer's fee becomes the lawyer's client.
Send Pat weekly reports but leave the plea decision to Rob.
Decline the payment, because a lawyer may never accept fees from anyone other than the client.
Take the payment only with Rob's informed consent, and give Pat no control or confidences.
Accept the payment and follow Pat's instructions if Pat signs a written fee agreement.
oe: The client is Rob. Paying the fee doesn't make Pat a client or give him control; Rule 1.8(f) and Rule 5.4(c) say so.
Rob hasn't consented to sharing information, so the reports would violate Rule 1.6 and Rule 1.8(f)(3).
Third-party payment is permitted when Rule 1.8(f)'s conditions are met.

Correct. Rule 1.8(f) allows a lawyer to accept payment from someone other than the client only if (1) the client gives informed consent, (2) there is no interference with the lawyer's independent judgment or the client-lawyer relationship, and (3) information is protected under Rule 1.6. Rule 5.4(c) also bars a payor from directing the lawyer's judgment, and the plea is Rob's decision under Rule 1.2(a).
A fee agreement doesn't authorize the payor to control the case or receive confidences; Rule 1.8(f) protects the client, not the payor.
questions.e: Rule 1.8(f): accept compensation from a third party only with (all required) (1) the client's informed consent, (2) no interference with the lawyer's independent judgment or the relationship, and (3) protection of the client's information under Rule 1.6; see also Rule 5.4(c).

questions.area: Concurrent Clients: The Concurrent Client Rule (MR 1.7)
questions.tag: MR 1.7(a)(1): suing a current client on an unrelated matter
questions.q: Lawyer Lana's firm represents Gorman Grocers in a commercial lease dispute. A new client, Pia, asks Lana to sue Gorman for a slip-and-fall injury unrelated to the lease. Lana has never worked on the lease matter, which is handled by her partner. May Lana take Pia's case?
o: Only if she reasonably believes she can serve both and both give informed consent, confirmed in writing.
Yes, because the slip-and-fall claim is not substantially related to the lease dispute the firm is handling.
Yes, because Lana personally has never worked on the lease matter, which her partner handles alone.
No, because a lawyer may never sue a current client, even with the consent of both clients.
Yes, if the firm first withdraws from the lease matter so that Gorman becomes a former client.
oe: Correct. Suing a current client, even on an unrelated matter, is direct adversity under Rule 1.7(a)(1) (Rule 1.7, Comment [6]). Through Rule 1.10(a) the firm's client is Lana's client too. The conflict is consentable under Rule 1.7(b) if she reasonably believes she can provide competent and diligent representation to each and both consent in writing.
"Substantially related" is the former-client test of Rule 1.9(a). For a current client, any direct adversity is a conflict under Rule 1.7(a)(1).
Rule 1.10(a) imputes the conflict of any lawyer in the firm to all of them, so Gorman's representation by her partner binds Lana.
Direct adversity is ordinarily consentable under Rule 1.7(b); only claims between clients in the same litigation are barred outright by Rule 1.7(b)(3).
Dropping a current client to take an adverse matter is the "hot potato" problem: courts generally still treat the dropped client as current.
questions.e: Direct adversity to a current client on any matter is a Rule 1.7(a)(1) conflict; it requires the Rule 1.7(b) conditions, including each affected client's informed consent, confirmed in writing, and is imputed firm-wide by Rule 1.10(a).

questions.area: Concurrent Clients: The Concurrent Client Rule (MR 1.7)
questions.tag: MR 1.7(b)(3): claims between clients in the same litigation
questions.q: Driver Ava and passenger Ben were both injured when a truck hit Ava's car. They ask Lawyer Cruz to represent both of them against the trucking company. Cruz learns that Ava had been texting while driving, so Ben has a strong claim against Ava too. Both clients say they want Cruz to represent them jointly against the trucking company and also want Ben to keep his claim against Ava in the same suit. May Cruz represent both on those terms?
o: No, because one client's claim against another in the same suit can't be consented to.
Yes, if both clients give informed consent, confirmed in writing, after Cruz explains the risks to each.
Yes, because Ava and Ben share the same interest in recovering from the trucking company.
No, because a lawyer may never represent two plaintiffs in the same lawsuit.
Yes, if Cruz reasonably believes he can present Ben's claim against Ava fairly.
oe: Correct. Rule 1.7(b)(3) makes a conflict nonconsentable when the representation involves "the assertion of a claim by one client against another client represented by the lawyer in the same litigation or other proceeding before a tribunal."
Consent cures many conflicts, but not one Rule 1.7(b)(3) forbids: a claim by one client against another in the same litigation.
Their shared claim against the trucking company doesn't erase the direct adversity created by Ben's claim against Ava in the same case.
Joint representation of co-plaintiffs is common and permitted when their interests are aligned or the conflict is consented to (Rule 1.7, Comment [23]).
The reasonable-belief test is Rule 1.7(b)(1). Rule 1.7(b)(3) is a separate condition that can't be met here.
questions.e: Rule 1.7(b) requires all four: (1) reasonable belief in competent and diligent representation of each, (2) not prohibited by law, (3) no claim by one client against another in the same litigation, and (4) informed consent, confirmed in writing, from each affected client.

questions.area: Concurrent Clients: The Concurrent Client Rule (MR 1.7)
questions.q: Lawyer Dax represents spouses Ely and Fern jointly in setting up a family business. Before the representation began, Dax explained that information either spouse shared would be shared with both. Later Ely privately tells Dax that he plans to transfer the business's best contracts to a company he secretly controls. Ely asks Dax to keep this from Fern. What should Dax do?
o: Keep Ely's secret, because Rule 1.6 forbids revealing one client's confidence to anyone, including the co-client.
Continue representing both and say nothing, because Ely hasn't yet carried out his plan.
Tell Ely he cannot keep it from Fern, and that Dax may have to withdraw if Ely won't let him share it.
Report Ely's plan to the police, because diverting business contracts is a crime.
Represent Fern alone against Ely from now on, since Fern is the innocent spouse.
oe: In a joint representation in which the clients agreed to share information, Rule 1.7, Comment [31] says each client is entitled to information bearing on the shared matter.
Staying silent would favor Ely over Fern; the conflict has become a Rule 1.7(a)(2) material limitation, and Dax cannot keep representing both on those terms.

Correct. Rule 1.7, Comment [31] says that in a joint representation each client has a right to be informed of anything bearing on the representation that might affect that client's interests, and the lawyer should tell the clients at the outset that information will be shared and that the lawyer will have to withdraw if one client asks that material information be kept from the other.
Nothing suggests a crime that a Rule 1.6(b) exception would cover; the issue is the joint clients' agreement and the conflict between them.
Dax would be adverse to Ely, a former client, in the same matter, which Rule 1.9(a) forbids without Ely's informed consent.
questions.e: In a joint representation, the lawyer should explain at the start that information will be shared and that one client's demand for secrecy will force withdrawal (Rule 1.7, Comments [30]–[31]); the attorney-client privilege generally doesn't protect communications between co-clients in later disputes between them.

questions.area: Concurrent Clients: The Concurrent Client Rule (MR 1.7)
questions.q: Lawyer Gail represents Client Hope in an appeal pending before the state supreme court, arguing that a certain statute of limitations runs from discovery of the injury. At the same time, Gail is asked to argue the opposite reading of the same statute for Client Ira in another appeal before the same court. Which statement best describes the situation?
o: There is no conflict, because a lawyer may always argue inconsistent legal positions for different clients.
There is a conflict only if Hope and Ira are adverse parties in the same case.
There is a nonconsentable conflict, because a lawyer may never take opposite legal positions in the same court.
There is no conflict unless Gail learned confidential information from Hope that would help Ira.
There is a conflict if arguing one side significantly risks limiting her advocacy for the other.
oe: Comment [24] says "ordinarily," not always; arguing both sides of the same issue to the same court creates a significant risk of material limitation.
Comment [24] recognizes positional conflicts between clients who are not adverse parties at all.
A positional conflict is a Rule 1.7(a)(2) conflict that may be consentable under Rule 1.7(b), though here the lawyer may not reasonably believe she can serve both.
The positional-conflict problem is about effectiveness of advocacy, not confidential information.

Correct. Rule 1.7, Comment [24] says ordinarily a lawyer may take inconsistent legal positions in different tribunals, but a conflict exists if there is a significant risk that the lawyer's action on behalf of one client will materially limit her effectiveness for the other, as when a decision in one case will create precedent likely to weaken the other client's position. Arguing both sides to the same court is a classic case.
questions.e: Positional conflicts (Rule 1.7, Comment [24]): inconsistent legal positions for different clients are usually fine, but there is a Rule 1.7(a)(2) conflict when there is a significant risk that the lawyer's work for one will materially limit her effectiveness for the other, such as arguing both sides before the same court.

questions.area: Former and Prospective Clients: The Successive Client Rule (MR 1.9, 1.18(c))
questions.q: Three years ago Lawyer Jan represented Client Kenco in negotiating a long-term supply contract with Lumco, learning Kenco's cost structure and pricing strategy. Jan's work for Kenco ended. Lumco now asks Jan to sue Kenco for breaching that same contract. Kenco objects. May Jan represent Lumco?
o: No, because the matter is the same and Lumco's interests are materially adverse to her former client's.
Yes, because Kenco is a former client, and the duty of loyalty ends when the representation ends.
Yes, if Jan promises not to use any of Kenco's confidential information in the case.
Yes, because three years have passed, so the information Jan learned is stale.
No, because a lawyer may never be adverse to a former client in any matter.
oe: Correct. Rule 1.9(a) forbids representing another person in "the same or a substantially related matter in which that person's interests are materially adverse to the interests of the former client unless the former client gives informed consent, confirmed in writing." Suing to enforce the very contract she negotiated is the same matter, and Kenco won't consent.
Loyalty to a former client continues in a limited form: Rule 1.9(a) bars switching sides in the same or a substantially related matter.
A promise doesn't cure a Rule 1.9(a) conflict. Only the former client's informed consent, confirmed in writing, does.
The passage of time can matter to whether information is still significant (Rule 1.9, Comment [3]), but suing over the very contract she negotiated is the same matter.
Rule 1.9(a) applies only to the same or substantially related matters; unrelated adverse matters are allowed.
questions.e: Rule 1.9(a): no representation materially adverse to a former client in the same or a substantially related matter without the former client's informed consent, confirmed in writing; matters are substantially related if they involve the same transaction or dispute or there is a substantial risk that confidential information would materially advance the new client's position (Comment [3]).

questions.area: Former and Prospective Clients: The Successive Client Rule (MR 1.9, 1.18(c))
questions.q: Lawyer Mo formerly represented Nova Corp. in a regulatory matter. Mo now represents Oak Inc. in an unrelated contract suit against Nova. In preparing the case, Mo relies on information about Nova's financial troubles that he learned while representing Nova, which has since been reported widely in the business press. Is Mo subject to discipline?
o: Yes, because a lawyer may never use a former client's information against it.
No, because he may use former-client information that has become generally known.
Yes, because suing a former client is direct adversity that requires the former client's consent.
No, because a lawyer's duties to a former client end with the representation.
Yes, unless Mo first discloses the information to Oak and obtains Nova's consent.
oe: Rule 1.9(c)(1) allows use of information that has become generally known.

Correct. Rule 1.9(c)(1) bars using information relating to a former representation to the former client's disadvantage "except as these Rules would permit or require with respect to a client, or when the information has become generally known." The new matter is unrelated, so Rule 1.9(a) isn't triggered.
Direct adversity is a current-client concept under Rule 1.7. With a former client, only the same or substantially related matters need consent under Rule 1.9(a).
Rule 1.9(c) continues to protect a former client's information after the representation ends; Mo is safe only because this information is generally known.
Rule 1.9(c)(2) forbids revealing former-client information except as the Rules permit; generally known status permits use, not consent-free disclosure of other information.
questions.e: Rule 1.9(c): a lawyer may not (1) use a former client's information to its disadvantage unless the Rules permit it or the information has become generally known, or (2) reveal it except as the Rules permit or require.

questions.area: Former and Prospective Clients: The Successive Client Rule (MR 1.9, 1.18(c))
questions.q: Wife Una meets for an hour with Lawyer Pax about divorcing her husband Vic and tells him about hidden assets and her plans for the custody fight. She decides not to hire Pax. A month later Vic asks Pax's partner, Quinn, to represent him in the divorce. Pax took no steps to limit what Una told him. Una won't consent. May Quinn represent Vic?
o: Yes, because Una never became Pax's client, so no conflict exists.
Yes, if the firm screens Pax from the matter and gives Una written notice.
No, because a lawyer may never represent a person adverse to someone who consulted the firm.
No, because Pax got significantly harmful information, and his conflict is imputed to Quinn.
Yes, because Rule 1.18 conflicts are personal to the lawyer who met the prospective client.
oe: Rule 1.18 protects prospective clients even when no relationship forms, and its conflict rule in Rule 1.18(c) applies here.
Screening works under Rule 1.18(d)(2) only if the lawyer took reasonable measures to limit the information he received; Pax didn't.

Too broad. Rule 1.18(c) applies only if the lawyer received information that could be significantly harmful in the same or a substantially related matter, and Rule 1.18(d) offers consent or screening.

Correct. Rule 1.18(c) bars Pax from representing Vic in the same matter because he received information from Una that could be significantly harmful to her, and the conflict is imputed to his firm. Rule 1.18(d)(2) screening is available only if Pax took reasonable measures to avoid exposure to more information than reasonably necessary, which he did not.
Rule 1.18(c) says that if a lawyer is disqualified, no lawyer in the firm may knowingly undertake the matter, except as Rule 1.18(d) provides.
questions.e: Rule 1.18(c) disqualifies a lawyer (and the firm) from a materially adverse representation in the same or a substantially related matter if he received significantly harmful information; Rule 1.18(d) cures it by both clients' written informed consent, or by screening if the lawyer took reasonable measures to limit what he learned, with no fee share and prompt written notice.

questions.q: Associate Raj worked on defending Sol Corp. in a pending product-liability case at his old firm. He then joins Tally & Ward, which represents the plaintiffs against Sol in that same case. Tally & Ward immediately screens Raj from the case, ensures he gets no part of the fee from it, and promptly sends Sol written notice describing the screen. Sol moves to disqualify the firm. Under the Model Rules, may Tally & Ward continue?
o: No, because a lawyer who switched sides in the same case taints the entire new firm, and screening can't cure it.
No, unless Sol gives informed consent, confirmed in writing, to the firm's continued representation.
Yes, because Raj's conflict arose at his prior firm and he was timely screened with the required notice.
Yes, because conflicts of associates are never imputed to their firms.
Yes, but only if Raj also promises Sol that he won't discuss the case with anyone at the firm.
oe: Under the Model Rules, Rule 1.10(a)(2) permits screening even for a lateral who worked on the same matter. Some states are stricter, but the Model Rule allows it.
Consent is one way to cure imputation (Rule 1.10(c)), but Rule 1.10(a)(2) screening is an independent route that doesn't require Sol's consent.

Correct. Rule 1.10(a)(2) does not impute a lateral lawyer's Rule 1.9 conflict that arises from association with a prior firm if (i) he is timely screened and apportioned no part of the fee, (ii) written notice is promptly given to the former client, and (iii) certifications of compliance are provided as the Rule requires.
Rule 1.10(a) imputes the conflicts of all lawyers associated in a firm, partners and associates alike.
A promise is not what the Rule requires; it requires a timely screen, no fee share, written notice, and certifications.
questions.e: Rule 1.10(a)(2): a lateral lawyer's Rule 1.9 conflict from a prior firm isn't imputed if (all required) (i) he is timely screened and gets no part of the fee, (ii) the former client gets prompt written notice, and (iii) certifications of compliance are provided; Rule 1.0(k) defines "screened."

questions.q: Lawyer Tia, a partner at a 40-lawyer firm, has strong personal religious objections to a defendant's position in a case the firm is handling. Her objections might affect her own work on it, but she has no role in the case, and the lawyers handling it don't share her views. Must the firm decline or withdraw from the case?
o: Yes, because Rule 1.10(a) imputes every lawyer's conflict to all the other lawyers associated in the firm.
No, because her personal-interest conflict doesn't significantly risk limiting the other lawyers.
Yes, unless the client gives informed consent, confirmed in writing, after learning of Tia's views.
No, but only if the firm formally screens Tia under Rule 1.0(k).
Yes, because a partner's views are attributed to the whole partnership.
oe: Rule 1.10(a)(1) excepts personal-interest conflicts that don't significantly risk limiting the other lawyers.

Correct. Rule 1.10(a)(1) does not impute a prohibition "based on a personal interest of the disqualified lawyer" that "does not present a significant risk of materially limiting the representation of the client by the remaining lawyers in the firm." Rule 1.10, Comment [3] gives a lawyer's strong political beliefs as an example.
No consent is needed when the conflict isn't imputed in the first place under Rule 1.10(a)(1).
Screening is required for lateral Rule 1.9 conflicts under Rule 1.10(a)(2), not for a non-imputed personal-interest conflict.
Imputation turns on the risk to the representation by the others, not on who holds what title in the firm.
questions.e: Rule 1.10(a) imputes conflicts within a firm except (1) personal-interest conflicts that don't significantly risk limiting the other lawyers, and (2) lateral Rule 1.9 conflicts handled by a proper screen and notice.

questions.tag: MR 1.10(b): after the tainted lawyer leaves
questions.q: Lawyer Uma represented Client Vito in a dispute with Wexco while she was at Firm Alpha. Uma left Alpha and took Vito and his file with her to her new firm; no one remaining at Alpha worked on Vito's matter or learned any of his confidential information. Wexco now asks Alpha to sue Vito in a matter substantially related to Uma's old work. May Alpha take the case?
o: No, because the matter is substantially related to Uma's former representation of Vito at Alpha.
No, because Vito is still a former client of Alpha, and Rule 1.9(a) forbids adversity in a substantially related matter.
Yes, but only if Alpha screens the lawyers who handle the new case from Uma.
Yes, because no lawyer remaining at Alpha has information protected by Rules 1.6 and 1.9(c) that is material to the matter.
No, unless Uma consents in writing to Alpha's representation of Wexco.
oe: A substantial relationship alone isn't enough under Rule 1.10(b); a remaining lawyer must also have material protected information.
Vito was never personally represented by the remaining lawyers, and Rule 1.10(b) specifically governs the firm's position once the lawyer who represented him has left.
Uma no longer works at Alpha, so there's nothing to screen; Rule 1.10(b) asks only whether remaining lawyers have material protected information.

Correct. Rule 1.10(b) lets a firm, after a lawyer leaves, represent a person adverse to a client the departed lawyer represented, unless the matter is the same or substantially related and any lawyer remaining in the firm has material information protected by Rules 1.6 and 1.9(c). Both conditions are needed to disqualify, and the second is missing.
The departed lawyer's consent isn't required; Rule 1.10(b) depends on what the remaining lawyers know.
questions.e: Rule 1.10(b): after a lawyer leaves, the old firm may be adverse to the client she represented unless (all required to disqualify) (1) the matter is the same or substantially related and (2) a remaining lawyer has material information protected by Rules 1.6 and 1.9(c).

questions.area: Addressing Conflicts: Abstention, Consent, and Conflict Checks
questions.q: Lawyer Xena is asked to represent both the buyer and the seller in the sale of a family farm. They are siblings who dislike each other, disagree sharply about the price, and each wants Xena to push for better terms. Both say they will sign any consent she puts in front of them. Which statement best describes whether Xena may represent both?
o: She may, if both siblings give informed consent, confirmed in writing.
She may, because the siblings aren't adverse parties in litigation before a tribunal.
She may not, because she can't reasonably believe she can serve both well.
She may not, because a lawyer may never represent both sides of any transaction.
She may, if she charges each sibling half her usual fee.
oe: Consent comes last. If a disinterested lawyer would conclude the clients shouldn't agree (Rule 1.7, Comment [15]), the conflict isn't consentable, no matter what the clients sign.
Rule 1.7(b)(3) is only one of the conditions; Rule 1.7(b)(1)'s reasonable-belief test independently bars this representation.

Correct. Under Rule 1.7(b)(1), a conflict is consentable only if the lawyer reasonably believes she can provide competent and diligent representation to each client. Rule 1.7, Comment [28] says common representation is improper where the clients' interests are fundamentally antagonistic and contentious negotiation is expected.
Too broad. Common representation of parties to a transaction can be proper when their interests are generally aligned and the lawyer can serve both (Rule 1.7, Comment [28]).
Fee arrangements have nothing to do with whether the conflict is consentable.
questions.e: A conflict is consentable only if all of Rule 1.7(b)(1)–(3) are met; the reasonable-belief test of Rule 1.7(b)(1) is objective (Comments [14]–[15]), and fundamentally antagonistic clients in contentious negotiation can't be represented jointly (Comment [28]).

questions.area: Addressing Conflicts: Abstention, Consent, and Conflict Checks
questions.q: Lawyer Yuri represents Client Zed in a contract dispute against Acme. Yuri's brother-in-law is Acme's general counsel and will direct Acme's defense. Yuri asks Zed to sign a form saying, "I consent to any conflicts of interest my lawyer may have," without explaining the relationship. Zed signs. Is Zed's consent effective?
o: Yes, because the consent is in a writing signed by the client.
Yes, because a family relationship with opposing counsel is not a conflict of interest.
No, because Zed was not told of the relationship and its risks, so his consent was not informed.
No, because a conflict arising from a family relationship can never be waived by the client.
Yes, because Zed is presumed to understand the risks of signing any document his lawyer presents.
oe: A signed writing satisfies the "confirmed in writing" form, but not the substance: consent is informed only after disclosure of the material risks and alternatives.
A close family relationship with the lawyer for the adverse party can be a Rule 1.7(a)(2) personal-interest conflict (Rule 1.7, Comment [11]).

Correct. Rule 1.7(b)(4) requires informed consent, which Rule 1.0(e) defines as agreement after the lawyer has communicated adequate information and explanation about the material risks of, and reasonably available alternatives to, the proposed course of conduct. A blanket consent to unnamed conflicts gives none (Rule 1.7, Comments [18]–[20]).
Rule 1.7, Comment [11] treats such conflicts as consentable with the client's informed consent.
There is no such presumption. The burden is on the lawyer to give the information that makes consent informed (Rule 1.0(e)).
questions.e: Informed consent (Rule 1.0(e)) requires the lawyer to explain the material risks of and reasonable alternatives to the proposed course of conduct; a blanket consent to undisclosed conflicts is ineffective, as Sheppard Mullin shows for an advance waiver that failed to disclose a known conflict.

questions.area: Addressing Conflicts: Abstention, Consent, and Conflict Checks
questions.q: Big Bank, a sophisticated client with its own in-house legal department, hires Law Firm Delta for regulatory advice. Delta's engagement letter, reviewed by Big Bank's general counsel, asks Big Bank to waive in advance any conflict arising from Delta representing other clients against the bank in future litigation unrelated to Delta's work for it. Big Bank signs. Two years later, Delta wants to sue Big Bank for another client in an unrelated matter. Is the advance waiver likely to be effective?
o: No, because a client can never consent to a conflict before it arises.
No, because a waiver of future conflicts is effective only if it names the specific future adverse client.
Yes, likely, because Big Bank is a sophisticated client that was independently advised.
Yes, because any signed advance waiver is binding, whatever the client's sophistication.
Yes, and it would also permit Delta to sue Big Bank in matters substantially related to Delta's regulatory work.
oe: Rule 1.7, Comment [22] expressly allows advance waivers in appropriate circumstances.
Identifying the type of future conflict helps, but Comment [22] says a general waiver can be effective for an experienced, independently advised client, especially as to unrelated matters.

Correct. Rule 1.7, Comment [22] says advance consent is more likely effective when the client is an experienced user of the legal services involved and is reasonably informed about the risk, particularly when the client is independently represented by other counsel in giving consent and the consent is limited to future conflicts unrelated to the subject of the representation.
Comment [22] makes effectiveness depend on how well the client understood the material risks; a general waiver from an unsophisticated client is ordinarily ineffective.
Comment [22] contemplates waivers of unrelated future conflicts; a substantially related matter raises confidentiality concerns and the Rule 1.7(b) conditions that a general waiver doesn't satisfy.
questions.e: Advance waivers (Rule 1.7, Comment [22]) are judged by how well the client understood the material risks; they work best for experienced, independently advised clients and for unrelated future matters, and never cure a nonconsentable conflict.

questions.area: The Government Lawyer's Client, Conflicts, and Extra Duties
questions.q: Assistant District Attorney Bo prosecutes a man for burglarizing the home of Victim Cam. Cam calls Bo several times a week, insisting that Bo take her calls as "my lawyer," and demands that Bo refuse any plea deal. Which statement best describes Bo's relationship with Cam?
o: Cam is not his client; Bo represents the government but should deal with her fairly.
Cam is Bo's client, because the prosecution is brought to vindicate the injury she suffered in the burglary.
Cam is Bo's client for the limited purpose of deciding whether the state should accept a plea.
Cam is a prospective client to whom Bo owes the duties of Rule 1.18.
Cam is not Bo's client, and Bo may therefore ignore her communications entirely.
oe: Correct. A prosecutor's client is the government (the state or "the people"), not the crime victim. Witnesses, helpers and victims are not clients even when the lawyer works closely with them. Bo should make clear that he is not Cam's lawyer (Rule 4.3) while giving appropriate weight to her views and any statutory victim's rights.
A prosecutor represents the sovereign. The victim is an interested person, not the client, so she cannot direct the prosecution.
There is no such limited relationship; plea decisions belong to the prosecutor exercising the government's discretion.
Cam is not consulting Bo about forming a client-lawyer relationship; she is a victim-witness in the government's case.
Bo should still treat Cam fairly, correct any misunderstanding about his role (Rule 4.3), and honor any victim's-rights laws.
questions.e: Government lawyers represent a government entity (Rule 1.13, Comment [9]); prosecutors represent the sovereign, not the victim, and must avoid misleading victims and witnesses about their role (Rule 4.3).

questions.q: As a lawyer at the state environmental agency, Ali personally and substantially handled the agency's enforcement action against Brightco for polluting a river. Ali has now joined a private firm, which Brightco asks to defend it against a citizens' suit over the same pollution. The agency has not consented to Ali's participation. Which statement is correct?
o: Neither Ali nor the firm may represent Brightco, because Ali's conflict is imputed to the firm under Rule 1.10(a).
Ali may work on the case, because he is now representing a private client in a different lawsuit from the agency's enforcement action.
Ali may work on the case if Brightco gives informed consent, confirmed in writing.
The firm may represent Brightco only if Ali consents in writing to the screen.
Ali may not work on the case, but the firm may if Ali is timely screened, gets no part of the fee, and the agency gets prompt written notice.
oe: Former government lawyers are governed by Rule 1.11, not Rule 1.10 (Rule 1.10(d)); Rule 1.11(b) allows screening.
"Matter" in Rule 1.11(e) covers the same set of facts involving specific parties; the citizens' suit over the same pollution by Brightco is the same matter.
The consent that matters under Rule 1.11(a)(2) is the government agency's, not the private client's.
The screen's validity doesn't depend on Ali's consent; it depends on timeliness, the fee bar and written notice to the agency under Rule 1.11(b).

Correct. Rule 1.11(a)(2) bars Ali from a matter in which he participated personally and substantially as a public employee unless the agency gives informed consent, confirmed in writing. Rule 1.11(b) lets the firm proceed if he is timely screened, apportioned no part of the fee, and written notice is promptly given to the agency.
questions.e: Rule 1.11(a): a former government lawyer may not represent a private client in a matter in which he participated personally and substantially, unless the agency gives informed consent, confirmed in writing; Rule 1.11(b) lets his firm proceed with a timely screen, no fee share, and prompt written notice to the agency.

questions.q: Lou served as a law clerk to Judge Mara and worked extensively on the briefs and draft opinion in a pending contract case between Pell Corp. and Quorum Inc. Near the end of her clerkship, Lou interviews with the firm representing Pell. Which statement is correct?
o: Lou may not interview with the firm while the case is pending, even if she tells Judge Mara first.
Lou may interview after notifying the judge, but can't later work on the case without consent.
Lou may interview without telling Judge Mara, because a law clerk is not a judicial officer.
Lou may interview and, if hired, work on the Pell case, because a law clerk makes no decisions.
Lou may interview only if Quorum, the opposing party, consents in writing.
oe: Judges and arbitrators may not negotiate employment with lawyers in their pending matters, but Rule 1.12(b) makes a specific exception for law clerks who first notify the judge.

Correct. Rule 1.12(b) lets a law clerk negotiate for employment with a party or lawyer in a matter in which the clerk is participating personally and substantially, but only after the clerk has notified the judge. Rule 1.12(a) then bars her from representing anyone in that matter unless all parties give informed consent, confirmed in writing; her new firm can screen her under Rule 1.12(c).
Rule 1.12(b) requires the clerk to notify the judge before negotiating employment.
Rule 1.12(a) expressly covers law clerks who participated personally and substantially in the matter.
The condition for a law clerk's negotiation is notice to the judge, not the parties' consent.
questions.e: Rule 1.12(a) bars former judges, arbitrators, mediators, other neutrals and law clerks from matters in which they participated personally and substantially, absent all parties' written informed consent; Rule 1.12(b) lets a law clerk negotiate employment only after notifying the judge; Rule 1.12(c) permits screening by the firm.

questions.q: Prosecutor Pip is trying a theft case. Before trial she learns that the store clerk who identified the defendant told a detective he "wasn't completely sure" of his identification. Pip believes the defendant is guilty and that the statement is too weak to change the outcome, so she doesn't disclose it. Is Pip subject to discipline?
o: No, because the statement is not material, so Brady v. Maryland doesn't require its disclosure.
No, because a prosecutor need disclose only evidence that she believes is credible.
Yes, but only if the defendant is convicted and the statement later comes to light.
Yes, because she must timely disclose information tending to negate guilt.
No, unless the defense specifically requested statements of the store clerk.
oe: Brady sets a constitutional floor with a materiality requirement. Rule 3.8(d) is broader: it requires disclosure of anything that tends to negate guilt.
Rule 3.8(d) doesn't let the prosecutor screen out exculpatory information because she discounts it.
The duty is to make timely disclosure; the violation occurs when the prosecutor withholds the information, whatever the verdict.

Correct. Rule 3.8(d) requires timely disclosure of "all evidence or information known to the prosecutor that tends to negate the guilt of the accused or mitigates the offense." It has no materiality limit, so it reaches further than the constitutional Brady standard, which asks whether the evidence would likely change the outcome.
Rule 3.8(d) requires disclosure without a specific request.
questions.e: Rule 3.8(d) requires timely disclosure of all information tending to negate guilt or mitigate the offense (and, at sentencing, unprivileged mitigating information), without Brady's materiality limit, unless a protective order relieves the prosecutor.

questions.tag: MR 3.8(c): waiver from an unrepresented accused
questions.q: Prosecutor Rick meets with an accused, Sal, who has not yet been appointed counsel. Rick tells Sal that if he waives his right to a preliminary hearing today, the state will consider a lighter charge later. Sal signs the waiver. Is Rick subject to discipline?
o: No, because Sal signed the waiver voluntarily and could have asked for a lawyer first.
No, because a preliminary hearing is not a constitutional right.
Yes, but only if Rick knew Sal would later be found indigent.
No, because Rule 3.8(c) applies only after formal charges have been filed in court.
Yes, because he sought a pretrial-rights waiver from an unrepresented accused.
oe: Rule 3.8(c) forbids seeking the waiver from an unrepresented accused at all; voluntariness doesn't cure it.
Rule 3.8(c) names the preliminary hearing as an example of the important pretrial rights it protects, whatever its constitutional status.
Rule 3.8(c) applies to any unrepresented accused, whether or not he is indigent.
Rule 3.8(c) protects the "accused," and Sal is accused; Rule 3.8(b)'s right-to-counsel duty applies too.

Correct. Rule 3.8(c) says a prosecutor shall not "seek to obtain from an unrepresented accused a waiver of important pretrial rights, such as the right to a preliminary hearing." Rule 3.8(b) also requires reasonable efforts to assure the accused has been advised of the right to counsel and given a reasonable opportunity to obtain it.
questions.e: Rule 3.8 adds duties for prosecutors, including (a) probable cause for charges, (b) reasonable efforts to assure the accused is advised of the right to counsel, and (c) no seeking waivers of important pretrial rights from an unrepresented accused.

questions.area: The Lawyer as Counselor and Neutral (MR 2.1, 2.3, 2.4, 3.9)
questions.q: Client Tara asks Lawyer Uri whether she may legally evict an elderly tenant who has lived in her building for 30 years. The eviction is lawful. Uri tells her so, and adds that evicting the tenant in midwinter may hurt her standing in a small town where she runs a business, and that he thinks it would be unkind. Tara didn't ask for his views on anything but the law. Was Uri's advice proper?
o: Yes, because a lawyer may refer to moral, economic, social and political factors in giving advice.
No, because a lawyer must confine his advice to the legal question the client asked.
No, because a lawyer's moral views are a personal interest that creates a conflict under Rule 1.7(a)(2).
Yes, but only because the eviction would harm a vulnerable third party.
Yes, and Uri must refuse to handle the eviction if Tara proceeds against his advice.
oe: Correct. Rule 2.1 requires candid advice based on independent professional judgment and provides that "a lawyer may refer not only to law but to other considerations such as moral, economic, social and political factors, that may be relevant to the client's situation." Rule 2.1, Comment [5] allows a lawyer to offer advice the client hasn't asked for when it is in the client's interest.
Rule 2.1 permits advice on non-legal considerations relevant to the client's situation, and Comment [5] permits volunteering advice in the client's interest.
Sharing a moral view in candid advice is what Rule 2.1 contemplates; it isn't a conflict unless the lawyer's beliefs would materially limit the representation.
The permission in Rule 2.1 doesn't depend on harm to a third person; moral, economic, social and political factors may always be mentioned when relevant.
The decision is Tara's under Rule 1.2(a). Uri may withdraw under Rule 1.16(b)(4) if he finds the action repugnant, but he isn't required to.
questions.e: Rule 2.1: a lawyer must exercise independent judgment and give candid advice, and may refer to moral, economic, social and political factors; offering unsolicited advice is appropriate when it is in the client's interest (Comment [5]).

questions.tag: MR 3.4(a): physical evidence of a crime
questions.q: Defense lawyer Vera's client, charged with armed robbery, brings her the gun he says he used and asks her to "make it disappear." Vera's state law requires turning over physical evidence of a crime that comes into a lawyer's possession. Which course is proper?
o: Vera may keep the gun in her office safe, because it came to her through a privileged communication.
Vera should return the gun to the client and tell him not to discuss it with anyone.
Vera must destroy the gun to protect her client's Fifth Amendment rights.
Vera may examine the gun without altering it, but she must then turn it over to the authorities as the law requires.
Vera must turn the gun over and also disclose everything the client told her about the robbery.
oe: The privilege protects communications, not physical evidence. Keeping the gun would unlawfully conceal evidence in violation of Rule 3.4(a).
Returning evidence so that it can be hidden or destroyed is assisting in obstructing access to evidence, in violation of Rule 3.4(a) and Rule 1.2(d).
Destroying evidence violates Rule 3.4(a) and the criminal law; the client's rights don't permit it.

Correct. Rule 3.4(a) forbids unlawfully obstructing access to evidence or concealing material with potential evidentiary value. Rule 3.4, Comment [2] says a lawyer may take temporary possession of physical evidence for a limited examination that won't alter it, and applicable law may require turning it over to the police.
Turning over the evidence doesn't require revealing the client's communications, which remain protected by Rule 1.6 and the privilege.
questions.e: Rule 3.4(a) bars unlawfully obstructing access to, altering, destroying or concealing evidence; a lawyer may briefly examine physical evidence without altering it but must turn it over when the law requires (Rule 3.4, Comment [2]), without disclosing the client's communications.

questions.q: Lawyer Wade receives an email from opposing counsel that plainly was meant for opposing counsel's client: it discusses the client's settlement limit. Wade realizes the mistake after reading the first two lines. What do the Model Rules require Wade to do?
o: Delete the email without reading further and say nothing to anyone.
Read the entire email and use it to his client's advantage, because the other side waived privilege.
Return the email and certify to the court that he has not read any of it.
Promptly notify the sender that he received the email.
Notify his own client first and follow the client's instructions about the email.
oe: Deleting may be wise or required by other law, but the Rule itself requires prompt notice to the sender.
Rule 4.4(b) requires notice to the sender regardless, and whether privilege was waived is a question of other law, not something the lawyer may assume.
The Model Rule requires notice. Court rules or other law may impose more, but Rule 4.4(b) itself doesn't require certification to a court.

Correct. Rule 4.4(b) requires a lawyer who receives a document or electronically stored information relating to the client's representation, and knows or reasonably should know it was inadvertently sent, to "promptly notify the sender." Rule 4.4, Comment [2] says whether he must return or delete it, or may read on, is for other law; Comment [3] leaves voluntary return to his judgment.
The duty to notify the sender belongs to the lawyer; it doesn't depend on the client's wishes.
questions.e: Rule 4.4(b): a lawyer who receives a document or ESI he knows or reasonably should know was inadvertently sent must promptly notify the sender; whether to return, delete or read it is for other law and the lawyer's judgment (Comments [2]–[3]).

questions.q: Defense lawyer Xia represents a city councilman charged with bribery. Reporters gather outside the courthouse after the arraignment. Which of the following statements may Xia properly make?
o: "The prosecution's star witness failed a lie-detector test, so the jury shouldn't believe him."
"My client passed a polygraph exam, which proves he never took a dime."
"I personally know my client is innocent, and anyone on the jury will see that too."
"My client denies the charges and will plead not guilty; the next hearing is set for May 3."
"The prosecutor's office has a grudge against my client, and the DA once took a bribe himself."
oe: Rule 3.6, Comment [5] lists the results of tests and the credibility of a witness as subjects likely to be materially prejudicial; polygraph results are typically inadmissible as well.
Statements about tests and their results are among those Comment [5] says are likely to have a material prejudicial effect in a criminal case.
Opinions about guilt or innocence are listed in Rule 3.6, Comment [5] as likely to prejudice a proceeding, especially when aimed at the jury pool.

Correct. Rule 3.6(b) lets a lawyer state, without elaboration, the claim, offense or defense involved (Rule 3.6(b)(1)) and the scheduling or result of any step in litigation (Rule 3.6(b)(4)). A bare denial and the announced plea are the defense involved.
This is far outside the Rule 3.6(b) safe harbor and, if false or reckless, could also violate Rule 8.2(a) or Rule 8.4(c).
questions.e: Rule 3.6(a) bars extrajudicial statements the lawyer knows or reasonably should know will be disseminated and have a substantial likelihood of materially prejudicing a proceeding; Rule 3.6(b) lists safe statements (claim, defense, public record, scheduling), and Rule 3.6(c) permits a limited reply to recent adverse publicity.

questions.q: Lawyer Yan negotiated a contract for Client Zia and was the only person present when the other side's CEO orally agreed to a key price term. The other side now denies the term, and Yan is the only witness who can prove it. The case is going to a jury trial. May Yan serve as trial counsel?
o: No, unless disqualifying him would work substantial hardship on Zia, but another lawyer in his firm may try the case.
Yes, if Zia gives informed consent, confirmed in writing, to Yan serving as both advocate and witness.
Yes, because Yan's testimony would help his own client, not hurt her.
No, and no lawyer in Yan's firm may try the case either, because his disqualification is imputed.
No, and Yan must also withdraw from all pretrial work on the case.
oe: Correct. Rule 3.7(a) bars a lawyer from acting as advocate at a trial in which he is likely to be a necessary witness unless the testimony relates to an uncontested issue, concerns the nature and value of legal services, or disqualification would work substantial hardship. Rule 3.7(b) lets others in his firm act as advocate unless Rule 1.7 or 1.9 precludes it.
Rule 3.7(a) protects the tribunal and the opposing party as well as the client; client consent is not one of its exceptions.
The Rule applies whenever the lawyer is likely to be a necessary witness, whether his testimony helps or hurts the client.
Rule 3.7(b) expressly lets other lawyers in the firm act as advocate unless a Rule 1.7 or 1.9 conflict precludes it.
Rule 3.7(a) restricts acting as advocate "at a trial"; courts applying it generally let the lawyer-witness keep doing pretrial work.
questions.e: Rule 3.7(a) bars the advocate-witness at trial unless (any one suffices) (1) the issue is uncontested, (2) the testimony concerns the nature and value of legal services, or (3) disqualification would work substantial hardship; under Rule 3.7(b) the lawyer's firm colleagues may usually try the case.

questions.q: Defendant Abe insists on testifying that he was at a movie when the crime occurred. Defense lawyer Bree doesn't know he is lying, but she strongly suspects it, because his story has changed twice. Which statement best describes Bree's options?
o: She must let him testify, because she doesn't know his testimony is false.
She may refuse to call Abe, because she reasonably believes his testimony is false.
She must disclose her suspicion to the court before Abe takes the stand.
She must withdraw, because she cannot ethically present testimony she suspects is false.
She may let Abe testify only in narrative form, without asking him questions.
oe: Correct. Rule 3.3(a)(3) lets a lawyer refuse to offer evidence she reasonably believes is false "other than the testimony of a defendant in a criminal matter." Rule 3.3, Comment [9] says that unless the lawyer knows the testimony will be false, she must honor the defendant's decision to testify. Knowledge can be inferred from circumstances (Rule 1.0(f)), but suspicion is not knowledge.
The reasonable-belief option in Rule 3.3(a)(3) expressly excludes a criminal defendant's own testimony.
There's no duty to disclose a mere suspicion; the remedial-measures duty in Rule 3.3(a)(3) applies once the lawyer knows evidence is false.
Rule 3.3, Comment [9] directs her to honor the client's decision; suspicion doesn't compel withdrawal.
The narrative approach, where some jurisdictions allow it, is a response to known perjury; it isn't required for a defendant whose testimony the lawyer only suspects is false.
questions.e: A lawyer may refuse to offer evidence she reasonably believes is false, except a criminal defendant's own testimony, which she may refuse only if she knows it is false (Rule 3.3(a)(3), Comment [9]); knowing false evidence requires remedial measures.

questions.tag: MR 3.3(a)(3), (c): remedial measures after false testimony
questions.q: In a civil trial, Client Cleo testifies on direct that she never received a warning letter. Lawyer Dov knows the testimony is false, because Cleo showed him the letter last month. After court, Cleo refuses to correct her testimony. What must Dov do?
o: Keep the false testimony confidential, because Rule 1.6 protects what Cleo told him.
Withdraw from the representation at once and say nothing to the court about the testimony.
Wait and correct the testimony only if the other side discovers the letter.
Disclose the falsity to opposing counsel, but not to the court.
Take reasonable remedial measures, including disclosure to the court if necessary.
oe: Rule 3.3(c) overrides Rule 1.6 for false evidence offered before a tribunal.
Withdrawal alone may not undo the effect of the false evidence (Rule 3.3, Comment [10]); if it doesn't, disclosure is required.
The duty is triggered when Dov knows the evidence is false; it continues until the conclusion of the proceeding (Rule 3.3(c)) and doesn't wait on the opponent.
The remedy runs to the tribunal, which is being misled. Telling only the opponent doesn't satisfy Rule 3.3(a)(3).

Correct. When a lawyer comes to know that his client offered material false evidence, Rule 3.3(a)(3) requires reasonable remedial measures, including, if necessary, disclosure to the tribunal. Rule 3.3(c) makes the duty apply even if it requires disclosing information otherwise protected by Rule 1.6. Rule 3.3, Comment [10] says to remonstrate first, then seek withdrawal if that will undo the effect, then disclose.
questions.e: Rule 3.3(a)(3) and (c): if a lawyer comes to know his client or witness offered material false evidence, he must take reasonable remedial measures (remonstrate, seek withdrawal, then disclose to the tribunal if necessary), even if that reveals Rule 1.6 information, until the proceeding concludes.

questions.q: Lawyer Eli is arguing a motion in a state trial court. He knows of a recent decision of the state's supreme court that is directly adverse to his position. Opposing counsel hasn't cited it in her brief. Must Eli disclose the case?
o: No, because it is opposing counsel's job to find authority that supports her client.
No, unless the judge specifically asks the lawyers whether any adverse authority exists on the issue.
Yes, and he must concede that the case controls the outcome of the motion.
Yes, because it is directly adverse controlling authority the other side hasn't cited.
Yes, but only if the adverse case was decided by a federal court rather than a state court.
oe: Rule 3.3(a)(2) places the duty on the lawyer when opposing counsel has not disclosed directly adverse controlling authority.
The duty doesn't depend on a question from the bench.
Disclosure is required; concession is not. Rule 3.3, Comment [4] lets him argue the authority doesn't apply or should be overruled.

Correct. Rule 3.3(a)(2) forbids knowingly failing "to disclose to the tribunal legal authority in the controlling jurisdiction known to the lawyer to be directly adverse to the position of the client and not disclosed by opposing counsel." He may still argue that the case is distinguishable or wrongly decided.
The test is controlling authority in the jurisdiction; for a state trial court, the state's supreme court is controlling.
questions.e: Rule 3.3(a)(2): disclose directly adverse legal authority in the controlling jurisdiction that opposing counsel hasn't disclosed; the lawyer may still argue it should be distinguished or overruled (Comment [4]).

questions.tag: MR 5.1(c): supervisor's knowledge and failure to act
questions.q: Partner Faye supervises Associate Gabe. Faye learns that Gabe told a client last week that a motion had been filed when it had not, and that the filing deadline is in two days, so the harm can still be avoided. Faye does nothing. The deadline passes and the client's claim is barred. Is Faye subject to discipline for Gabe's misconduct?
o: Yes, because she knew in time to avoid the harm and took no remedial action.
No, because a lawyer is responsible only for her own violations of the Rules.
No, because Faye did not order or ratify Gabe's misrepresentation.
Yes, because a partner is vicariously responsible for every violation by a lawyer she supervises.
No, because only the client can complain about a missed deadline, through a malpractice suit.
oe: Correct. Rule 5.1(c)(2) makes a lawyer responsible for another lawyer's violation if she has direct supervisory authority (or is a partner or manager) and "knows of the conduct at a time when its consequences can be avoided or mitigated but fails to take reasonable remedial action."
Rule 5.1(c) creates responsibility for another lawyer's violation in two situations, and knowledge plus failure to remediate is one.
Ordering or ratifying is the Rule 5.1(c)(1) route; Rule 5.1(c)(2) separately covers knowing of the conduct and failing to remediate.
Rule 5.1(c) doesn't impose strict vicarious liability; Faye is responsible because she knew and failed to act in time.
A malpractice claim may lie too, but discipline under Rule 5.1(c)(2) is independent of civil liability.
questions.e: Rule 5.1(c): a lawyer is responsible for another lawyer's violation if she (1) orders or, with knowledge, ratifies it, or (2) is a partner, manager or direct supervisor who knows of it when its consequences can be avoided or mitigated and fails to take reasonable remedial action (any one suffices).

questions.q: Lawyer Hana runs a busy immigration practice and has her paralegal, Ike, meet new clients and fill out their forms. Hana has never told Ike that client information is confidential, has no office policies on confidentiality, and doesn't review his work. Ike posts a client's story, with identifying details, on social media. Hana didn't know about the post until a client complained. Is Hana subject to discipline?
o: No, because she did not know about Ike's post and did not order or ratify it.
No, because only lawyers are bound by the duty of confidentiality in Rule 1.6.
Yes, because she made no reasonable efforts to supervise her paralegal.
Yes, because a lawyer is strictly liable in discipline for anything her nonlawyer assistants do.
No, unless the client suffered financial harm from the post.
oe: Knowledge and ratification matter under Rule 5.3(c), which makes the lawyer answer for the nonlawyer's conduct itself; Hana's own duty under Rule 5.3(a)–(b) to set measures and supervise was breached regardless.
The Rules don't bind nonlawyers directly, which is why Rule 5.3 makes the supervising lawyer responsible for reasonable measures and supervision.

Correct. Rule 5.3(a) and (b) require a lawyer with managerial or direct supervisory authority to make reasonable efforts to ensure that a nonlawyer's conduct is compatible with the lawyer's professional obligations. Rule 5.3, Comment [2] stresses instruction and supervision on confidentiality. Hana's own failure to supervise is the violation, even though she didn't know of the post.
Rule 5.3 isn't strict liability; Hana is subject to discipline because she made no reasonable efforts.
Discipline under Rule 5.3 doesn't depend on proving financial harm to the client.
questions.e: Rule 5.3: managers must have measures giving reasonable assurance that nonlawyers' conduct fits the lawyer's obligations, supervisors must make reasonable efforts to ensure it, and a lawyer answers for a nonlawyer's conduct that would violate the Rules if she orders, ratifies or knowingly fails to remediate it.

questions.area: Duties to the Firm, Changing Jobs, and Selling a Practice (MR 1.17, 5.7)
questions.tag: MR 1.17: sale of a law practice
questions.q: Lawyer Jill is retiring from private practice in her state and agrees to sell her entire estate-planning practice to Lawyer Kurt. Kurt plans to raise the hourly rates of Jill's clients by 20 percent to recover the purchase price. Jill sends each client written notice of the sale but doesn't mention that the clients may take their files elsewhere. Which statement is correct?
o: The sale is proper, because Jill is selling her entire practice and ceasing private practice.
The sale is improper, because a lawyer may never sell the goodwill of a law practice to another lawyer.
The sale is proper if each client consents in a writing signed by the client before the sale closes.
The sale is improper only because Jill must notify the disciplinary authority before selling.
The sale is improper, because the notice is incomplete and fees may not rise because of the sale.
oe: Those meet Rule 1.17(a) and (b), but the notice and fee requirements of Rule 1.17(c) and (d) aren't met.
Rule 1.17 expressly permits the sale of a law practice, including its goodwill, on its conditions.
Rule 1.17(c) presumes consent after 90 days without objection; signed consents aren't required, and they wouldn't permit a fee increase.
Rule 1.17 requires notice to clients, not to disciplinary authorities.

Correct. Rule 1.17(c) requires written notice to each client of the proposed sale, the client's right to retain other counsel or take possession of the file, and the fact that consent will be presumed if the client doesn't act or object within 90 days. Rule 1.17(d) forbids increasing fees by reason of the sale.
questions.e: Rule 1.17 permits selling a practice if (all required) (a) the seller ceases private practice in the area or jurisdiction, (b) the entire practice or area of practice is sold, (c) clients get written notice of the sale, their right to other counsel and their files, and the 90-day presumption of consent, and (d) fees aren't increased because of the sale.

questions.area: Duties to the Firm, Changing Jobs, and Selling a Practice (MR 1.17, 5.7)
questions.q: Lawyer Lia wants to open a firm with her friend Max, an accountant, who would put up the money, own half the firm, and serve as its business manager. Max would not give legal advice and would not tell Lia how to handle cases. Under the Model Rules, may Lia form the firm?
o: Yes, because Max won't direct Lia's professional judgment or give legal advice.
Yes, if the firm's clients give informed consent to Max's ownership interest.
Yes, because accountants are licensed professionals bound by their own rules of conduct.
No, because a lawyer may not practice in a firm in which a nonlawyer owns an interest.
No, because a lawyer may not employ nonlawyers in management roles at a law firm.
oe: Lack of control is necessary but not sufficient. Rule 5.4(b) and (d)(1) bar nonlawyer ownership outright under the Model Rules.
Rule 5.4's limits on nonlawyer ownership can't be waived by client consent.
Rule 5.4 makes no exception for other licensed professionals.

Correct. Rule 5.4(b) forbids forming a partnership with a nonlawyer if any of its activities consist of the practice of law, and Rule 5.4(d)(1) bars practicing in a professional corporation or association authorized to practice law for a profit if a nonlawyer owns any interest in it. The Model Rules don't allow this even if the nonlawyer won't direct the lawyer's judgment.
Lawyers may employ nonlawyer managers, such as office administrators (Rule 5.3); the problem is ownership.
questions.e: Rule 5.4 protects professional independence: (a) no fee sharing with nonlawyers (with narrow exceptions), (b) no partnership with a nonlawyer in practicing law, (c) no letting a payor or recommender direct the lawyer's judgment, and (d) no for-profit practice with nonlawyer owners, directors or controllers.

questions.q: Lawyer Nia, outside counsel to Omnico, is investigating possible bribery by Omnico's sales staff. She interviews salesman Pete, who seems to think Nia is there to help him. Nia believes Pete may be one of the wrongdoers. What must Nia do before questioning him?
o: Nothing, because Pete is an employee of Omnico, and Omnico is the client she represents.
Advise Pete that he should not answer any questions until he has his own lawyer.
Tell Pete she represents Omnico, not him, and that Omnico controls the privilege.
Promise Pete that what he says will be kept confidential from Omnico's management.
Agree to represent Pete as well, so that his statements are privileged.
oe: Because Pete's interests may be adverse to Omnico's and he misunderstands her role, Rule 1.13(f) and Rule 4.3 require her to clarify it.

She may tell him he may wish to get his own lawyer, but advising him not to cooperate would be legal advice to an unrepresented person whose interests conflict with her client's (Rule 4.3) and would work against Omnico.

Correct. Rule 1.13(f) requires a lawyer for an organization to explain the identity of the client when she knows or reasonably should know the organization's interests are adverse to the constituent's. Rule 1.13, Comment [10] describes the Upjohn warning: she represents the company, not him, he may wish to get his own lawyer, and the privilege belongs to the company, which may waive it.
She can't promise that: the information belongs to the client, Omnico, which controls the privilege.
Representing Pete would create a Rule 1.7 conflict with Omnico in an investigation where their interests may be adverse.
questions.e: Rule 1.13(a): the organization is the client; under Rule 1.13(f) (and Rule 4.3), when a constituent's interests may be adverse, the lawyer must explain that she represents the organization (the Upjohn warning: company's lawyer, company's privilege, consider your own counsel).

questions.q: In-house lawyer Quin learns that Omnico's vice president of sales is booking fake sales to inflate the quarter's revenue, which violates securities law and is likely to cause the company substantial injury. Quin raises it with the VP, who refuses to stop. What must Quin do?
o: Report the VP directly to the Securities and Exchange Commission.
Do nothing further, because she has already advised the VP that his conduct is unlawful.
Report it up to higher authority in Omnico, including the board if warranted.
Resign immediately, because she may not continue to work for a company engaged in fraud.
Warn the company's outside auditors, because they are relying on false revenue figures.
oe: Reporting out is permitted only under Rule 1.13(c), after the organization's highest authority fails to address a clear violation; the first step is reporting up.
Rule 1.13(b) requires her to proceed in the organization's best interest; when the VP persists, that ordinarily means going up the ladder.

Correct. Under Rule 1.13(b), when a lawyer knows a constituent is acting in violation of law that might be imputed to the organization and is likely to cause it substantial injury, she must proceed as reasonably necessary in the organization's best interest and, unless she reasonably believes it isn't necessary, refer the matter to higher authority, including the highest authority that can act.
Resignation may come later, but Rule 1.13(b) first requires her to act in the organization's best interest by reporting up.
Disclosure outside the company is governed by Rule 1.13(c) and Rule 1.6(b); it isn't the first step Rule 1.13(b) requires.
questions.e: Rule 1.13(b): a lawyer who knows of a constituent's violation likely to cause the organization substantial injury must act in its best interest and, unless reasonably believed unnecessary, report up to higher authority, including the highest authority; reporting out is permitted only under Rule 1.13(c).

questions.tag: MR 1.13(c)–(d): reporting out and its exception
questions.q: Lawyer Rae was hired by Omnico's board to defend the company in a government investigation of accounting fraud. During her work she learns details of the past fraud, and the board refuses to take any action. May Rae reveal the fraud to the government under Rule 1.13(c)?
o: No, because she was hired to defend Omnico against the very violation at issue.
Yes, because the board, as the highest authority, refused to act on a clear violation of law.
Yes, and she must, because a lawyer must report organizational fraud to the government.
No, because a lawyer may never reveal an organizational client's information without the board's consent.
Yes, but only to the extent the information shows the fraud is still continuing.
oe: Correct. Rule 1.13(d) says paragraph (c) "shall not apply with respect to information relating to a lawyer's representation of an organization to investigate an alleged violation of law, or to defend the organization or an officer, employee or other constituent associated with the organization against a claim arising out of an alleged violation of law."
That meets Rule 1.13(c)'s trigger, but Rule 1.13(d) removes the reporting-out permission for lawyers hired to defend the organization against the alleged violation.
Rule 1.13(c) is permissive ("may"), and here it doesn't apply at all because of Rule 1.13(d).
Rule 1.13(c) does permit reporting out in some circumstances, regardless of Rule 1.6; it is unavailable here only because of Rule 1.13(d).
Rule 1.13(d) applies to defense and investigation counsel whatever the timing; the limit here is the role, not whether the fraud continues.
questions.e: Rule 1.13(c) permits reporting out (regardless of Rule 1.6) if the highest authority fails to address a clear violation of law reasonably certain to cause substantial injury to the organization; Rule 1.13(d) excludes lawyers hired to investigate or defend the alleged violation.

questions.area: Pro Bono, Appointments, and Public-Service Organizations (MR 6.1–6.5)
questions.tag: MR 6.2: court appointment and good cause
questions.q: A judge appoints Lawyer Sid to represent an indigent defendant charged with assaulting a police officer. Sid, a former officer, asks to be excused because he dislikes defendants who hurt police, though he admits he could represent the defendant competently and his feelings wouldn't affect his work. Is Sid's reason good cause to avoid the appointment?
o: Yes, because a lawyer may always decline a matter he finds distasteful.
Yes, because Sid's former employment creates a nonconsentable conflict of interest.
No, because a lawyer must accept every court appointment, whatever the reason for declining.
No, because his dislike won't impair his representation of the client.
Yes, if Sid instead agrees to do 50 hours of other pro bono work this year.
oe: A lawyer can usually decline private matters, but Rule 6.2 limits avoiding court appointments to good cause.
Past police work, without more, doesn't create a Rule 1.7 conflict that prevents him from representing the defendant.
Rule 6.2 does recognize good cause, including repugnance strong enough to impair the representation.

Correct. Rule 6.2 says a lawyer shall not seek to avoid an appointment except for good cause, such as when (a) it would violate the Rules or other law, (b) it would be an unreasonable financial burden, or (c) the client or cause is so repugnant to the lawyer as to be likely to impair the relationship or the lawyer's ability to represent the client. Sid admits his feelings won't affect his work.
Rule 6.1's aspirational pro bono goal isn't a substitute for an appointment; Rule 6.2 asks only whether good cause exists.
questions.e: Rule 6.2: don't seek to avoid an appointment except for good cause (any one suffices): (a) it would violate the Rules or other law, (b) unreasonable financial burden, or (c) the client or cause is so repugnant as to be likely to impair the relationship or representation.

questions.q: Lawyer Tad represents a buyer negotiating to purchase a small business. Which of the following statements by Tad to the seller's lawyer would most likely violate Rule 4.1?
o: "My client has an accountant's report showing the business lost money last year," when no such report exists.
"My client won't pay a penny more than $400,000," when the client has authorized up to $450,000.
"Frankly, this business isn't worth anything close to your asking price."
"My client is looking at several other businesses," when the client has looked at two.
"We think your client's projections are optimistic," when Tad privately thinks they're reasonable.
oe: Correct. Rule 4.1(a) forbids knowingly making a false statement of material fact or law to a third person. Inventing a document is a false statement of fact, not negotiation puffery.
Rule 4.1, Comment [2] says a party's intentions as to an acceptable settlement of a claim are ordinarily not taken as statements of material fact under generally accepted negotiation conventions.
Estimates of price or value are, under Comment [2], ordinarily not statements of material fact.
This is true, so it isn't a false statement at all; a lawyer need not volunteer how serious the other options are.
An opinion about projections in a negotiation is the kind of posturing that Comment [2] doesn't treat as a statement of material fact.
questions.e: Rule 4.1(a) bars knowingly false statements of material fact or law to third persons; under Comment [2], estimates of price or value and a party's settlement intentions are ordinarily not material facts, but invented facts or documents are.

questions.q: Lawyer Uma represents a seller of a house. During negotiations, Uma learns from her client, in confidence, that the basement floods every spring. The buyer hasn't asked about flooding. State law imposes no duty on a seller to disclose it, and the client hasn't used Uma's services to make any misrepresentation. Must Uma disclose the flooding to the buyer?
o: Yes, because a lawyer must disclose every material fact that the other side would want to know.
Yes, because failing to disclose a known defect is always a false statement under Rule 4.1(a).
No, because a lawyer never has a duty to disclose anything to a third person.
Yes, but only after withdrawing, so that the disclosure isn't made while she represents the seller.
No, because the client hasn't committed a fraud through Uma, and Rule 1.6 protects the information.
oe: Rule 4.1, Comment [1] says a lawyer generally has no affirmative duty to inform an opposing party of relevant facts.
Silence isn't a false statement unless it amounts to a misrepresentation, such as a half-truth; Uma has said nothing about flooding.
Too broad. Rule 4.1(b) imposes a duty in narrow circumstances, and a lawyer can't make misleading partial statements.
Withdrawal doesn't create a duty to disclose confidential information; Rule 1.6 continues to protect it.

Correct. Rule 4.1(b) requires disclosure of a material fact only when necessary to avoid assisting a client's criminal or fraudulent act, and then only if Rule 1.6 doesn't prohibit it. No fraud is involved on these facts, and Rule 1.6(a) protects the information.
questions.e: Rule 4.1(b) requires disclosure of a material fact only when necessary to avoid assisting a client's crime or fraud, and only if Rule 1.6 permits; otherwise a lawyer has no general duty to volunteer facts, but must not make misleading half-truths.
