questions.q: Lawyer Vic represents a homeowner suing a contractor, Wes, who is represented by counsel. Wes calls Vic directly, says his own lawyer is "useless," and asks to talk about settling. Wes says he consents to talking without his lawyer. May Vic discuss settlement with Wes?
o: Yes, because Wes initiated the call and consented to speaking without his lawyer.
Yes, so long as Vic tells Wes that he represents the homeowner and not Wes.
Yes, if Vic limits the conversation to settlement and avoids discussing the merits.
No, because the contact needs the consent of Wes's lawyer.
No, unless Vic first obtains a court order permitting the contact.
oe: The protected person's consent isn't enough; only the other lawyer's consent (or law or court order) authorizes the contact (Rule 4.2, Comment [3]).
Clarifying one's role is the rule for unrepresented persons under Rule 4.3; Wes is represented.
Settlement is part of "the subject of the representation"; Rule 4.2 bars the contact entirely.

Correct. Rule 4.2 forbids communicating about the subject of the representation with a person the lawyer knows is represented in the matter "unless the lawyer has the consent of the other lawyer." Rule 4.2, Comment [3] says the Rule applies even if the represented person initiates or consents to the communication.
A court order is one route, but the ordinary one is the other lawyer's consent. The choice isn't limited to a court order.
questions.e: Rule 4.2: in representing a client, don't communicate about the matter with a person you know is represented in it unless that person's lawyer consents or law or a court order authorizes it; the represented person's own consent or initiation doesn't matter (Comment [3]), but the parties may talk to each other directly (Comment [4]).

questions.q: Lawyer Xo represents an employee suing Yarrow Corp., which is represented by counsel, for workplace injuries. Xo wants to interview, without Yarrow's lawyer present, (1) the plant manager whose orders allegedly caused the injury and (2) a former maintenance worker who left Yarrow last year and saw the accident. Which interviews does Rule 4.2 forbid without Yarrow's counsel's consent?
o: Both interviews, because both people have information about the accident.
The interview with the plant manager only.
The interview with the former worker only, because he is no longer protected by Yarrow's counsel.
Neither interview, because only Yarrow's officers and directors are protected by Rule 4.2.
Neither interview, if Xo identifies herself and her client at the start.
oe: Rule 4.2 doesn't protect every employee with information, and Comment [7] says it doesn't reach former constituents.

Correct. Rule 4.2, Comment [7] protects a current constituent who supervises, directs or regularly consults with the organization's lawyer about the matter, has authority to obligate the organization, or whose act or omission may be imputed to it. The manager's orders may be imputed to Yarrow. Consent of the organization's lawyer is not required for a former constituent.
This reverses the rule: the current manager is protected, and the former worker isn't.
Comment [7] reaches beyond officers to any constituent whose act or omission may be imputed to the organization, such as this manager.
Identifying herself is what Rule 4.3 requires with unrepresented persons; it doesn't permit contact with a represented organization's protected constituent under Rule 4.2.
questions.e: For a represented organization, Rule 4.2, Comment [7] protects current constituents who supervise, direct or regularly consult with its lawyer about the matter, can obligate it, or whose conduct may be imputed to it; former constituents may be contacted, though the lawyer must not seek privileged information (Rule 4.4(a)).

questions.tag: MR 4.3: legal advice to an unrepresented person
questions.q: Lawyer Zane represents a landlord in a dispute with a tenant, Ana, who has no lawyer. Ana calls Zane and asks whether she has any legal defense to the landlord's claim for back rent. Which response is proper?
o: "Legally, you don't have any defense, so you should just pay what you owe."
"I'm a neutral lawyer handling this dispute, and I'll try to be fair to both of you."
"I represent your landlord, so I can't advise you; you may want your own lawyer."
"You might have a defense based on the landlord's failure to make repairs, but I can't say more."
"I can't talk to you at all unless your lawyer is on the line."
oe: That is legal advice to a person whose interests conflict with Zane's client's, which Rule 4.3 forbids.
Rule 4.3 forbids stating or implying that the lawyer is disinterested.

Correct. Rule 4.3 forbids giving legal advice to an unrepresented person, other than the advice to secure counsel, when the lawyer knows or reasonably should know that the person's interests conflict or may conflict with the client's. Zane must also make clear he isn't disinterested.
Even a partial suggestion about a defense is legal advice, and pointing out a defense to the client's opponent is also inconsistent with Zane's duties to his client.
Ana has no lawyer, so Rule 4.2 doesn't apply; Zane may talk to her, negotiate, and state his client's position, so long as he complies with Rule 4.3.
questions.e: Rule 4.3: when dealing with an unrepresented person, don't state or imply disinterest, correct misunderstandings of your role, and give no legal advice (other than to get a lawyer) if interests conflict or may conflict; stating facts or your client's position is permitted.

questions.tag: MR 1.2(d): advising on consequences vs. assisting
questions.q: Client Bo, a restaurant owner, asks Lawyer Cal how much he could save by paying his cooks in cash "off the books" and what the penalties would be if the state labor department found out. Which response by Cal is proper?
o: Help Bo set up a cash payroll, so long as Cal advises him that it is illegal.
Refuse to discuss the subject at all, because discussing illegal conduct is assisting it.
Explain the legal consequences, including penalties, but decline to help set it up.
Tell Bo how to keep the labor department from discovering the cash payments.
Report Bo to the labor department, because he has disclosed a plan to commit a crime.
oe: Advising that it's illegal doesn't permit assisting; setting up the payroll is assisting in conduct Cal knows is unlawful, which Rule 1.2(d) forbids.
Rule 1.2(d) expressly permits discussing the legal consequences of a proposed course of conduct.

Correct. Rule 1.2(d) forbids counseling or assisting a client in conduct the lawyer knows is criminal or fraudulent, but lets the lawyer "discuss the legal consequences of any proposed course of conduct with a client." Explaining the penalties is proper; helping Bo carry out the scheme is not.
Advice on avoiding detection is counseling the client to break the law, forbidden by Rule 1.2(d).
No Rule 1.6(b) exception applies to a plan that hasn't used Cal's services; disclosure would violate Rule 1.6(a).
questions.e: Rule 1.2(d): don't counsel or assist a client in conduct you know is criminal or fraudulent, but you may discuss the legal consequences of any proposed course of conduct and help the client test the law in good faith (Comment [12]).

questions.tag: MR 1.16(a)(4): client persists in using the lawyer's services
questions.q: Lawyer Dee is helping Client Eve with loan applications. Dee discovers that Eve has been inflating her income figures on the forms Dee prepares. Dee explains that she can't help with false applications and why, but Eve insists on submitting the inflated figures through Dee. Under the current Model Rules, what must Dee do?
o: Continue the representation, but remove her own name from the applications.
Withdraw only if she reasonably believes the fraud will cause substantial financial injury to the lender.
Report Eve to the lender, because a lawyer must disclose a client's fraud.
Continue, because a lawyer may withdraw for a client's fraud but is never required to.
Withdraw, because Eve persists in using her services to commit fraud.
oe: Continuing while the client uses her work to commit fraud is assisting fraud under Rule 1.2(d), and Rule 1.16(a)(4) requires withdrawal.
The withdrawal duty in Rule 1.16(a)(4) doesn't depend on the amount of injury; the "substantial injury" language belongs to the disclosure exceptions in Rule 1.6(b)(2)–(3).
Rule 1.6(b)(2) may permit disclosure where the client used the lawyer's services, but it doesn't require it; the mandatory duty here is withdrawal.
Permissive withdrawal is Rule 1.16(b)(2)–(3); Rule 1.16(a)(4) makes withdrawal mandatory when the client persists after the lawyer's warning.

Correct. Rule 1.16(a)(4), added in 2023, requires a lawyer to withdraw when the client "seeks to use or persists in using the lawyer's services to commit or further a crime or fraud, despite the lawyer's discussion pursuant to Rules 1.2(d) and 1.4(a)(5)." Continuing would also violate Rule 1.2(d).
questions.e: If a client seeks to use or persists in using the lawyer's services to commit a crime or fraud after the lawyer explains the limits (Rules 1.2(d), 1.4(a)(5)), the lawyer must decline or withdraw under Rule 1.16(a)(4); the lawyer may also consider disclosure under Rule 1.6(b)(2)–(3).

questions.area: Abusive Tactics, Threats, and Reporting Misconduct (MR 4.4(a), 8.3)
questions.q: Lawyer Fin learns from opposing counsel's own email, sent to Fin by mistake, that opposing counsel has been taking money from a client trust account to pay office rent. Fin's own client didn't give him this information, and it doesn't relate to Fin's representation of his client. Must Fin report opposing counsel?
o: No, because Fin learned of the conduct through an inadvertently sent email.
No, because a lawyer is required to report only misconduct he has personally witnessed.
Yes, because he knows of a violation that raises a substantial question about the lawyer's honesty and fitness.
Yes, but only after first confronting opposing counsel and giving him a chance to repay the money.
No, because the duty to report applies only to lawyers in the reporting lawyer's own firm.
oe: How Fin learned of it doesn't excuse the reporting duty; Rule 4.4(b) requires notice to the sender, but Rule 8.3(a) still applies.
Rule 8.3(a) turns on knowledge, which can come from any source, not personal observation.

Correct. Rule 8.3(a) requires a lawyer who knows that another lawyer has committed a violation of the Rules raising a substantial question as to that lawyer's honesty, trustworthiness or fitness to inform the appropriate professional authority. Misusing trust funds plainly qualifies. Fin should also notify the sender under Rule 4.4(b).
Rule 8.3(a) doesn't require confronting the other lawyer first or giving a chance to cure.
Rule 8.3(a) applies to "another lawyer," whether or not in the same firm.
questions.e: Rule 8.3(a): a lawyer who knows another lawyer committed a violation raising a substantial question as to honesty, trustworthiness or fitness must inform the appropriate professional authority; Rule 8.3(c) excepts information protected by Rule 1.6 and information gained in an approved lawyers assistance program.

questions.area: Abusive Tactics, Threats, and Reporting Misconduct (MR 4.4(a), 8.3)
questions.tag: MR 4.4(a): no substantial purpose other than to burden
questions.q: Lawyer Gil represents a defendant in a minor contract case. To pressure the plaintiff, Gil schedules the plaintiff's elderly mother, who has no knowledge of the dispute, for a full-day deposition in a city three hours from her home, and serves subpoenas on the plaintiff's employer for records that have nothing to do with the case. Is Gil subject to discipline?
o: No, because a lawyer may use any discovery the rules of civil procedure permit.
No, because Rule 4.4(a) protects only parties to the case, not their relatives or employers.
Yes, but only if a court first sanctions Gil for the discovery.
Yes, because he used means that have no substantial purpose other than to burden third persons.
No, because aggressive tactics are part of zealous advocacy for a client.
oe: Discovery that is permitted on its face still violates Rule 4.4(a) when its only substantial purpose is to burden third persons.
Rule 4.4(a) protects "third persons," which includes non-party witnesses and businesses.
Discipline doesn't depend on a court sanction; the two are independent.

Correct. Rule 4.4(a) forbids a lawyer, in representing a client, to "use means that have no substantial purpose other than to embarrass, delay, or burden a third person." The mother and the employer are third persons, and the discovery serves no legitimate purpose. Rule 3.4(d) and court sanctions may apply too.
Zeal doesn't excuse tactics with no substantial purpose other than to burden others (Rule 4.4(a)).
questions.e: Rule 4.4(a): don't use means with no substantial purpose other than to embarrass, delay or burden a third person, or methods of obtaining evidence that violate a person's legal rights; the same conduct may draw sanctions under FRCP 11, FRCP 26(g) or 28 U.S.C. § 1927.

questions.q: Lawyer Hoyt represents ten tenants suing a landlord over mold. The landlord offers a generous settlement on the condition that Hoyt agree never to represent any other tenant against the landlord. The tenants want Hoyt to accept. May Hoyt agree to the condition?
o: Yes, because the clients want the settlement and the decision to settle is theirs.
No, because he may not agree to a practice restriction in a settlement.
Yes, if the restriction is limited to a reasonable time and geographic area.
No, but the landlord's lawyer commits no violation by proposing it.
Yes, so long as Hoyt doesn't represent any other tenants against the landlord.
oe: The clients decide whether to settle, but Rule 5.6(b) forbids the lawyer from agreeing to this term even with their consent.

Correct. Rule 5.6(b) forbids a lawyer to participate in offering or making "an agreement in which a restriction on the lawyer's right to practice is part of the settlement of a client controversy." Rule 5.6, Comment [2] confirms that the Rule bars agreeing not to represent other persons as part of settling a client's claim; like the restrictions in Rule 5.6(a) (Comment [1]), such terms limit future clients' freedom to choose a lawyer.
Reasonableness limits apply in some contexts, but Rule 5.6(b) bars any practice restriction as part of a settlement.
Rule 5.6(b) bars participating "in offering or making" the agreement, so the landlord's lawyer who proposes it violates the Rule too.
Complying with the restriction doesn't make the agreement permissible.
questions.e: Rule 5.6: no agreement restricting a lawyer's right to practice (a) after leaving a firm or job (except retirement-benefit conditions) or (b) as part of settling a client controversy; both the offering and accepting lawyers violate Rule 5.6(b).

questions.tag: MR 7.3(b): live solicitation for pecuniary gain
questions.q: After a highway pileup, Lawyer Ivy goes to the hospital and approaches injured drivers in the emergency waiting room, offering to represent them on a contingent fee. One of the drivers is Ivy's college roommate. Is Ivy subject to discipline?
o: No, because she is offering truthful information about legal rights to people who need it.
Yes, as to every driver she approached, including her roommate.
No, because a contingent fee means she charges nothing unless the drivers recover.
No, unless one of the drivers had told her he didn't want to be solicited.
Yes, as to the strangers, because live solicitation for pecuniary gain is barred.
oe: Truthfulness doesn't save in-person solicitation for pecuniary gain; Rule 7.3(b) bars it because of the risk of undue influence.
Rule 7.3(b)(2) exempts persons with a family, close personal, or prior business or professional relationship with the lawyer.
A contingent fee is still pecuniary gain; Rule 7.3(b) applies.
That limit, in Rule 7.3(c)(1), applies to all solicitation; live person-to-person solicitation for gain is barred under Rule 7.3(b) regardless.

Correct. Rule 7.3(b) forbids live person-to-person contact to solicit professional employment when a significant motive is pecuniary gain, unless the person contacted is a lawyer, has a family, close personal or prior business or professional relationship with the lawyer, or routinely uses the type of legal services offered for business purposes. Her roommate has a close personal relationship; the strangers don't.
questions.e: Rule 7.3(b) bars live person-to-person solicitation for pecuniary gain except of (1) lawyers, (2) family, close personal, or prior business or professional contacts, or (3) routine business users of the services; Rule 7.3(c) bars any solicitation of people who have said no or that involves coercion, duress or harassment.

questions.q: Lawyer Jax's website says, truthfully, "We won $4 million for an injured worker last year." It doesn't mention that the case involved unusual facts and that most of the firm's cases settle for far less. Under the Model Rules, is the statement likely to be misleading?
o: No, because a statement that is literally true can never violate Rule 7.1.
No, because Bates and Zauderer give lawyers an absolute First Amendment right to advertise.
Yes, because lawyers may never mention past results in advertising.
Yes, because it may create unjustified expectations about results.
Yes, because any ad that mentions a dollar amount violates Rule 7.2.
oe: Rule 7.1 reaches truthful statements that are misleading because they omit necessary facts or create unjustified expectations.
Bates and Zauderer protect truthful, non-misleading lawyer advertising; states may still regulate misleading ads.
Too broad. Past results may be mentioned if not misleading; Rule 7.1, Comment [3] suggests qualifying language can prevent unjustified expectations.

Correct. Rule 7.1 forbids false or misleading communications, including truthful statements that omit facts needed to keep them from being misleading. Rule 7.1, Comment [3] says a truthful report of a lawyer's achievements on behalf of clients may be misleading if presented so as to lead a reasonable person to form an unjustified expectation; a disclaimer or qualifying language may cure it.
Rule 7.2 governs advertising mechanics, such as payment for recommendations and required contact information; it doesn't ban dollar figures.
questions.e: Rule 7.1 bars false or misleading communications about a lawyer's services, including truthful statements that omit facts or create unjustified expectations (Comment [3]); qualifying language may cure the risk, and Zauderer allows required disclosures to prevent deception.

questions.tag: MR 8.4(g): conduct related to the practice of law
questions.q: At a law firm's holiday party for its lawyers and staff, Partner Kip repeatedly makes demeaning jokes about a junior associate's national origin, after she asks him to stop. The firm says the party was a social event, not law practice. Is Kip subject to discipline under Rule 8.4(g)?
o: No, because a firm party is a social event, not the practice of law.
Yes, because harassment at a firm social event is conduct related to the practice of law.
No, because the First Amendment protects jokes, however offensive.
No, unless the associate files an employment discrimination claim against the firm.
Yes, but only because Kip, as a partner, is responsible for the firm's workplace under Rule 5.1.
oe: Rule 8.4, Comment [4] expressly reaches social activities in connection with the practice of law, such as a firm party.

Correct. Rule 8.4(g) forbids conduct the lawyer knows or reasonably should know is harassment or discrimination on the basis of, among other things, national origin, in conduct related to the practice of law. Rule 8.4, Comment [4] includes interacting with coworkers and participating in business or social activities in connection with the practice of law, and Comment [3] defines harassment to include derogatory or demeaning verbal conduct.
Burk notes the First Amendment debate over Rule 8.4(g), but under the Model Rule as written, demeaning harassment of a coworker at a firm event is covered.
Discipline under Rule 8.4(g) doesn't depend on a civil claim; Comment [3] says substantive antidiscrimination law may guide but doesn't limit it.
Kip's own conduct violates Rule 8.4(g); his responsibility doesn't depend on his management role.
questions.e: Rule 8.4(g) bars conduct the lawyer knows or reasonably should know is harassment or discrimination on listed bases in conduct related to the practice of law, which Comment [4] defines to include dealings with coworkers and firm social events; it doesn't limit accepting, declining or withdrawing under Rule 1.16 or legitimate advocacy.
